### Summary

I use some CircuitPython libraries for an Adafruit board. Typing with ty has been fine with the use of `circuitpython-stubs` but recently I encountered a missing attribute error when using the `adafruit-circuitpython-logging` library:

```sh
uv add adafruit-circuitpython-logging
```

```py
import adafruit_logging as logging

logger = logging.getLogger("mylog")
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
                ^^^^^^^^^^^^
error[[unresolved-attribute](https://ty.dev/rules#unresolved-attribute)]: 
  Module `adafruit_logging` has no member `ERROR`
   --> src/bikelib/fcan/core.py:250:21
    |
248 |     # Setup diagnostic logging.
249 |     logger = logging.getLogger("fcan")
250 |     logger.setLevel(logging.ERROR)  # logging.INFO
    |                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
251 |     logger.info("Requesting closed-loop control...")
    |
info: rule `unresolved-attribute` is enabled by default
```

The following alternative passes `ty check`, and the code runs correctly on-device:

```py
logger.setLevel(20)
```

Notes:
- The attribute `INFO` is defined in `adafruit_logging.py`.
- I do not see this issue with the python `logging` library, only the CircuitPython variant.


### Version

```text
ty 0.0.17 (8cec85718 2026-02-13)
adafruit_circuitpython_logging 5.6.0
```

body_text:
### Summary

**Feature**

I would like the following to work:

```py
from typing import assert_type

def _(foo: str | None) -> None:
    assert_type(["a", "b", foo] * bool(foo), list[str])
```

playground url: https://play.ty.dev/6b918b9f-39ce-4faf-a2be-ef6ab1a08107

As shown by the playground, unlike mypy, ty already does type-narrowing on `bool`, so I'm essentially asking to propagate that type narrowing to inline lists `__mul__`'ed with a typeguard.

**Pitch**

Let me quote @jaraco directly, as this is a pattern used a lot in his ecosystem (which includes setuptools): https://github.com/jaraco/jaraco.context/pull/16#discussion_r2967882086
> I very much prefer to use algebraic expressions over branching logic. The expressiveness of multiplying by a bool is important to the aesthetic of simplicity here.

### Summary

Not sure why you would ever do this, but if you do ty gets confused and makes an incorrect `__init__`
[Playground](https://play.ty.dev/50860f01-40f2-4f90-94f8-d39d84a875b7)
```py
from typing import reveal_type, Final, ClassVar
from dataclasses import dataclass, InitVar

@dataclass
class A:
    x: InitVar[ClassVar[int]]

# Runtime: TypeError: A.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'x'
reveal_type(A())
```
The fun part is that because of how `dataclass` works, if you swap the order to `ClassVar[InitVar[int]]` ty is now correct, since the `InitVar` checking only checks the top level. Also see https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html#init-only-variables

body_text:
### Summary

Consider this code:

```python
from typing import reveal_type

def untyped_one():
    return 1
def narrow_to_int[U: int](x: U) -> U:
    return x
reveal_type(narrow_to_int(untyped_one())) # Unknown
```

I think ty could handle this better: if the call to `narrow_to_int` is accepted in the first place, then ty has accepted that U is a subtype of `int`, and `ty`'s type algebra has intersection types.  So I think the right should be `Unknown & int`, and maybe that could be simplified to `int`.

This comes from https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/136#issuecomment-4194822089

FWIW, neither mypy nor pyright appear to do any better than ty here.

### Summary

1. New folder.
2. Create `test_requests.py`, run `uv venv`.

```python
import pathlib

import requests
```

3. Ask agent "go to definitions for requests import". As expected, it will fail.

```
● LSP(operation: "goToDefinition", symbol: "requests", in: "test_requests.py")                                                                                                  
  ⎿  Found 0 definitions     
No definition found. This may occur if the cursor is not on a symbol, or if the definition is in an external library not indexed by the LSP server.
```

4. Run `uv pip install requests`
5. Ask "go to definitions for requests import again" - it will fail with the same error, though venv is installed now.

So it appears as `ty server` is not picking up new dependencies as they get installed.
A workaround is to restart `ty` server, in Claude it means to run `/reload-plugins` (given that ty was installed from https://github.com/astral-sh/claude-code-plugins).

body_text:
### Question

In https://github.com/coherent-oss/coherent.test/issues/24, I'm exploring the possibility of using `ty` as the supported/recommended type checker for the [Coherent Build System](/coherent-oss/system). The main blocker (same as with mypy) is that `ty` expects all modules to have their package layout fully materialized in the file system, something the coherent system avoids in the [essential layout](https://github.com/coherent-oss/system/blob/main/essential-layout.md) to avoid unnecessary repetition.

Briefly, the essential layout puts modules for a package (namespace or otherwise) in the root of the repo. So for the [encutils project](/coherent-oss/encutils), `./__init__.py` represents the `encutils` Python module/package. In the [coherent.test project](/coherent-oss/coherent.test), `./__init__.py` represents the `coherent.test` package and `./monkey.py` represents the `coherent.test.monkey` module.

I'd like to use `ty` to perform type checks on these packages while still in their repo/source form, but when I try to do so, I get errors on relative imports:

```
error[unresolved-import]: Cannot resolve imported module `.`
 --> __main__.py:1:1
  |
1 | from . import core
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

I'd like a way, short of materializing the package's parent's, to indicate to `ty` something like:

> modules in `.` are the implementation of package X, where X is possibly a namespace package.

And/or

> treat the module `./__init__.py` as if it had been found in `coherent/test/`.

The coherent build system has been able to achieve this layout for Python imports using a [proxy](https://github.com/coherent-oss/coherent.build/blob/aff254318640f6e9404c1764b812432252ed01f5/backend.py#L85-L112) and pytest using a [monkeypatch](https://github.com/coherent-oss/coherent.test/blob/c381aaa524564174c6a7b678bcf2140cb5bf026c/monkey.py#L48-L53). A similar technique was used to [monkeypatch mypy](https://github.com/coherent-oss/coherent.test/blob/c381aaa524564174c6a7b678bcf2140cb5bf026c/monkey.py#L32-L45), but it [proved unsuccessful](https://github.com/coherent-oss/coherent.test/issues/23) when the code was pre-compiled.

Since `ty` is compiled rust, it'll need first-class support for this functionality.

What might it take for `ty` to honor the essential layout?

Thanks for your consideration.

When having a (data-)class as input to a function, it would be good to have the option to see on a hover of the type annotation, what attributes the class has to help writing the correct code.

In the issues #1351, #3072, this was already implemented when using the constructor of the class.

The current workaround is copying the attributes into a docstring for the class:
```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Example:
   """
   Attributes:
      first_attribute: str,
      second_attribute: int | None
   """
   first_attribute: str
   second_attribute: int | None,



def function_that_uses_the_class(arg: str, example: Example):
   ...
```

This is undesired, because it adds a lot of boilerplate and is errror prone, when changing things.

### Summary

https://play.ty.dev/19cdfcf5-e80b-43b1-840e-eebc6d31e446

`ty` reports one `type-assertion-failure`, with an inferred type of `Box[Unknown]`. mypy 2.3.1, pyright 1.1.411, and pyrefly 1.2.0 accept the example and infer `Box[int]`.

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Protocol, TypeVar, assert_type, overload

T = TypeVar("T", covariant=True)
S = TypeVar("S", bound=int)
T_contra = TypeVar("T_contra", contravariant=True)
T_co = TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True)


class SupportsAdd(Protocol[T_contra, T_co]):
    def __add__(self, other: T_contra, /) -> T_co: ...


class SupportsRAdd(Protocol[T_contra, T_co]):
    def __radd__(self, other: T_contra, /) -> T_co: ...


class Box(Protocol[T]):
    @overload
    def __radd__(self: Box[int], other: int, /) -> Box[int]: ...

    @overload
    def __radd__(  # type: ignore[misc]
        self: Box[T], other: SupportsAdd[T, S], /
    ) -> Box[S]: ...

    @overload
    def add(self: Box[T], other: SupportsRAdd[T, S]) -> Box[S]: ...

    @overload
    def add(self: Box[int], other: Box[int]) -> Box[int]: ...


def get_box() -> Box[int]:
    raise NotImplementedError


box = get_box()
assert_type(box.add(box), Box[int])
```

### AI Summary

When checking a concrete `Box[int]` argument, ty incorrectly keeps an overload involving a nested reverse-operation protocol and infers `Box[Unknown]`. Matching that overload would require the bounded type variable `S` to be `Box[int]`, so the overload should be rejected and the concrete `Box[int]` overload should be selected.

This appears related to #4366 (an incompatible protocol overload surviving overload resolution) and #4150 (a gradual generic being inferred during protocol assignability). Unlike #4055 and its duplicate #4195, there is no `Any` at the call site (or anywhere in this reproduction).

We now have pretty good diagnostics for unpacked assignments where every target is a `Name` expression. For example, on this code: ```py a: int a, b = "foo", "bar" ``` we emit this diagnostic:
Screenshot
But our diagnostics are still quite poor if any target on the left-hand side is an attribute or subscript expression. On this code: ```py class Foo: a: int Foo().a, b = "foo", "bar" wut: list[int] = [42] wut[0], b, = "foo", "bar" ``` we emit these diagnostics:
Screenshot
The diagnostic spans in particular are far from ideal: they don't give you any information about exactly which variable in the unpacking causes the problem. Ideally we'd do better here, but we left it out of scope of https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28041 since it's considerably more complex than for `Name` expressions.

body_text:
`missing-direct-dependency` doesn't check a local module's imports against the declarations of the PEP 723 script that imports it.

For example, `requests` installs `urllib3` transitively:

**`script.py`**
```python
# /// script
# dependencies = ["requests"]
# [tool.ty.environment]
# root = ["."]
# ///

import b
```

**`b.py`**
```python
import urllib3
```

With the script support from [astral-sh/ruff#28136](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28136), running:

```sh
TY_UV=scripts ty check script.py --error missing-direct-dependency
```

prints `All checks passed!`. Adding `import urllib3` directly to `script.py` reports the missing declaration.

Follow-up to [Micha's review comment](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28136#discussion_r3882114724).

A constructor call that matches no overload infers `Unknown` when the callee is a subclass, but the bare instance type when the callee is the class itself. Same error, same overload set — only the receiver differs.

```python
from typing import overload

class Box[T]:
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, code: int) -> "Box[int]": ...
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, code: str) -> "Box[str]": ...
    def __new__(cls, code): ...

class Sub(Box): ...

reveal_type(Box())  # `Box[T@Box]`
reveal_type(Sub())  # `Unknown`   <- expected `Sub`
```

Both lines raise `no-matching-overload`. I'd expect the subclass to recover the same way the class does, to `Sub`.

## What makes it fire

Bisected in pure user code — the condition is an overloaded `__new__` whose overloads have **differing** return types, none of them `Self`:

| overloads | `Box()` | `Sub()` |
|---|---|---|
| `-> Box[int]`, `-> Box[str]` | `Box[T@Box]` | **`Unknown`** |
| `-> Self`, `-> Self` | `Box[T@Box]` | `Sub` |
| `-> Box[int]`, `-> Box[int]` | `Box[int]` | `Box[int]` |
| non-generic, `-> Box`, `-> Box` | `Box` | `Box` |
| overloaded `__init__` instead of `__new__` | `Box` | `Sub` |
| single non-overloaded `__new__` | `Box[int]` | `Box[int]` |

Parameterizing the base (`class Sub(Box[int])`) does not change it. Overloads returning genuinely unrelated types (`-> A`, `-> B`) give `Unknown` for both, which seems right — a `Box()` really isn't a `Box` there. The asymmetry above is the part that looks wrong.

## In the standard library

`array.array` and `slice` hit this, because their `__new__` overloads return concrete `array[int]` / `slice[Any, _T, Any]`:

```python
import array
class S(array.array): pass

reveal_type(array.array())  # `array[_T@array]`
reveal_type(S())            # `Unknown`
reveal_type(S('i'))         # `array[int]`     (valid call, fine)
```

`range` is the contrast: its `__new__` overloads all return `Self`, so `class R(range): pass; R()` still reveals `R` despite raising the same `no-matching-overload`.

The knock-on effect is what we ran into: once `S()` is `Unknown`, member access on it resolves nothing, so `S().tobytes()` has no inferred type either. A one-argument mistake costs every type downstream of the call, not just the call.

## Version

`ty 0.0.78 (dca9f9873 2026-09-02)`, also reproduced on `ty@latest` via `uvx`.

body_text:
How to reproduce:

1. Initialize a new workspace with `uv init` (important, see below). Doesn't matter if I `uv sync` or not afterwards.
2. Open the workspace as a folder in VS Code.
3. Open, for example, the generated \_\_init\_\_.py and add `from collections.abc import Sequence` to it.
4. Place the cursor on `Sequence` and press F12 to navigate to its definition.

Expected result: I see the actual definition of `collections.abc.Sequence`, which is in the file "/usr/lib/python3.14/_collections_abc.py" on my system (or I see a typed stub definition from typeshed).

Actual result: The editor opens the file "/usr/lib/python3.14/typing.py" and just shows me an unhelpful alias:
```python
Sequence = _alias(collections.abc.Sequence, 1)
```

body_text:
### Summary

*This is an issue from an LSP perspective, though I suspect this is a duplicate for #1306 as a type checker perspective.*

When using stub files, LSP's find references from the `.py` implementation turn up empty.

## Minimal reproducer

```python
# a.pyi
class A: ...  # -> "find references" finds usage in b.py
```
```python
# a.py
class A:  # -> "find references" finds no references
    """Some documentation"""
    pass
```
```python
# b.py
from a import A
```

As far as I can tell, this is within the scope of expected usage for stub files. From the [typing specs](https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/distributing.html) : 

> [stub files] can provide type information for packages that do not wish to add them inline

 ( and later, as a recognized usage for type stubs)

> The package maintainer would like to add type information via stubs.

Note that *go to definition* (say, from `b.py`) still finds the `a.py` implementation, and *hover* still finds the documentation, so it's at least surprising that this doesn't hold for references.

## How other LSPs treat this

- `pyrefly` : same as `ty`
- `pyright` : same as `ty`
- `pylsp` : 
  - from `a.py`, only sees the `a.pyi` reference
  - from `a.pyi`, only sees the `a.py` reference (??)
  - from `b.py`, sees all occurrences of `A` in all three files

I'm surprised that none of those have the behavior that I would expect so maybe it's just me ?

(thank you for `ty`, it's a lovely tool ✨)
(Hopefully this is not me misconfiguring my LSPs and editor ✨)

Following up on astral-sh/ruff#19559, where @ntBre suggested opening a ty issue to discuss this.

I’d like an opt-in rule that discourages modules within a package from importing symbols through that package’s re-exports, requiring imports from the defining module instead.

When writing packages, I often re-export functions and classes in `__init__.py` to provide a convenient public API. Those imports are useful for external consumers, but using them internally can introduce circular imports and make dependencies harder to follow.

For example:

* `supercoolpkg/http_error.py` defines `HTTPError`.
* `supercoolpkg/__init__.py` explicitly re-exports it with `from .http_error import HTTPError as HTTPError`.
* `supercoolpkg/http_client.py` imports it with `from supercoolpkg import HTTPError`.

The proposed rule would flag the import in `http_client.py` and suggest `from supercoolpkg.http_error import HTTPError`. External consumers could continue using `from supercoolpkg import HTTPError`.

This differs from astral-sh/ty#200, which proposes an `implicit-reexport` rule for runtime files. Here, the re-export is explicit and intentional: the goal is to discourage internal use of it, regardless of whether it is declared through a redundant alias or `__all__`.

Would this make sense as a separate opt-in rule in ty?

body_text:
to my knowledge no existing linter or type checker is able to detect mistakes like this. for example:

```py
def get_values() -> list[int]:
    return [i for i in range(3)]

values = get_values()

assert 4 not in values # passes
assert 1 in values # passes
```

but if `get_values` is updated to return a `Generator` instead of a `list`, it can unintentionally break existing usages:

```py
from typing import Generator

def get_values() -> Generator[int]:
    return (i for i in range(3))

values = get_values()

assert 4 not in values # passes
assert 1 in values # fails because the generator has no more values to iterate
```

i've encountered issues like this several times, so it would be nice if ty had a rule for it.

ty reports a syntax error and infers `Unknown` for a forward reference whose body starts with whitespace. mypy and pyright both accept the identical file.

```python
from typing import List

a: "  List[int]" = []
b: "List[int]" = []

reveal_type(a)  # ty: `list[Unknown]`, mypy/pyright: `list[int]`
reveal_type(b)  # `list[int]` everywhere
```

```
error[invalid-syntax-in-forward-annotation]: Syntax error in forward annotation
 --> repro.py:3:5
  |
3 | a: "  List[int]" = []
  |     ^^---------
  |     |
  |     Expected an expression
help: Did you mean `typing.Literal["  List[int]"]`?
```

| | `a: "  List[int]"` |
|---|---|
| ty 0.0.81 (4edd7724a 2026-09-14) | `invalid-syntax-in-forward-annotation`, `list[Unknown]` |
| mypy 2.3.1 | `Revealed type is "list[int]"`, no error |
| pyright 1.1.414 | `Type of "a" is "List[int]"`, 0 errors |

## Mechanism

`parse_string_annotation` sends triple-quoted bodies to `Mode::ParenthesizedExpression` and everything else to `Mode::Expression` ([`crates/ruff_python_parser/src/lib.rs`](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/main/crates/ruff_python_parser/src/lib.rs#L228)):

```rust
if string.flags.is_triple_quoted() {
    parse_parenthesized_expression_range(source, range)
} else {
    parse_expression_range(source, range)
}
```

`Mode::Expression` starts the lexer in `State::AfterNewline` with `nesting = 0`, so `lex_token` runs `eat_indentation` on the first token and the two leading spaces lex as an `Indent`. Parsing the exact same range in each mode:

```
Mode::Expression:              Err(ExpectedExpression, 28..30)
Mode::ParenthesizedExpression: Ok(30..39)     // true in-file range of `List[int]`
```

The failure is total rather than degraded — `parse_string_annotation` returns `None`, so no expression inside the annotation is inferred at all, not just the outermost one.

## Why this case slipped through

astral-sh/ruff#9467 asked for quoted annotations to be parsed as if parenthesized. astral-sh/ruff#15387 closed it but scoped the change to triple quotes, citing python/typing-council#9. That council thread only settled newlines inside triple-quoted strings; leading whitespace in a single-quoted body was never raised there.

## PEP 484's test has already been overridden once, by this exact mechanism

PEP 484 is the only normative text here, and it is not ambiguous: the body must satisfy `compile(lit, '', 'eval')`, and `compile("  List[int]", '', 'eval')` raises `IndentationError`. PEP 563 restates the same test, and CPython agrees at runtime — `get_type_hints` raises `SyntaxError: Forward reference must be an expression`.

But the triple-quote rule appears in no PEP; python/typing#1578 added it to the spec in 2024. It admits bodies that fail that same test, because a leading newline raises `IndentationError` exactly as leading spaces do:

```python
a: """
   List[int]""" = []   # compile() -> IndentationError; ty infers list[int]
b: "  List[int]" = []  # compile() -> IndentationError; ty infers list[Unknown]
```

So the spec has already carved out one exception to PEP 484 for bodies that fail `compile()` on indentation. `b` is the same defect the carve-out was written to fix, and mypy and pyright both already read it that way.

## If you want the lenient behavior

Dropping the branch is the whole change:

```rust
let source = &source[..range.end().to_usize()];
parse_parenthesized_expression_range(source, range)
```

I measured the diagnostic delta on a spread of odd bodies; only the leading-whitespace ones change. `""`, `"   "`, `"int)"`, `"(int"`, `"int;"`, `"int "`, `"int, str"`, `"int if True else str"` and `" " "int"` all produce byte-identical output. `cargo test -p ruff_python_parser` (813 tests) and `cargo test -p ty_python_semantic` are green with the change.

Happy to open a PR. Equally happy if the answer is that the diagnostic should stay — in that case it may still be worth parsing the whitespace-stripped body so the contents keep types, rather than dropping the annotation wholesale.

### Summary

When an overloaded function is passed to a generic function that uses `ParamSpec`, ty does not resolve the overload against the actual arguments. It returns a union of the overload return types instead. mypy and pyright both resolve it correctly.

```py
from typing import Callable, Literal, overload, reveal_type

@overload
def f(*, flag: Literal[False]) -> str: ...
@overload
def f(*, flag: Literal[True] = ...) -> int: ...
def f(*, flag: bool = True) -> int | str:
    return 1 if flag else 'a'

def call[**P, T](fn: Callable[P, T], *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> T:
    return fn(*args, **kwargs)

reveal_type(f())      # ty: int         mypy: int   pyright: int
reveal_type(call(f))  # ty: str | int   mypy: int   pyright: int
```

The last line should be `int`. No `flag` argument is passed, so the second overload applies via its default.

The usual way to hit this is `Executor.submit`, whose first parameter is `Callable[P, T]`:

```py
takes_int(executor.submit(f).result())
# error[invalid-argument-type]: Expected `int`, found `str | int`
```

With three or more overloads ty sometimes picks the last overload's return type rather than a union, but the effect is the same.

This looks like the other half of #2383. That issue was closed when ParamSpec support landed, and the argument is indeed accepted now — but the return type is still wrong.

Impact: we evaluated ty on a ~1600-file codebase that is clean under mypy strict. This one pattern produces 437 of 689 diagnostics, because our database accessors are overloaded on a `Literal[bool]` flag that selects the return type, and they are usually called through `executor.submit`.

Possibly related: #2568, #3415, #2799.

### Version

When an overloaded function is passed to a generic function that uses `ParamSpec`, ty does not resolve the overload against the actual arguments. It returns a union of the overload return types instead. mypy and pyright both resolve it correctly.

```py
from typing import Callable, Literal, overload, reveal_type

@overload
def f(*, flag: Literal[False]) -> str: ...
@overload
def f(*, flag: Literal[True] = ...) -> int: ...
def f(*, flag: bool = True) -> int | str:
    return 1 if flag else 'a'

def call[**P, T](fn: Callable[P, T], *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> T:
    return fn(*args, **kwargs)

reveal_type(f())      # ty: int         mypy: int   pyright: int
reveal_type(call(f))  # ty: str | int   mypy: int   pyright: int
```

The last line should be `int`. No `flag` argument is passed, so the second overload applies via its default.

The usual way to hit this is `Executor.submit`, whose first parameter is `Callable[P, T]`:

```py
takes_int(executor.submit(f).result())
# error[invalid-argument-type]: Expected `int`, found `str | int`
```

With three or more overloads ty sometimes picks the last overload's return type rather than a union, but the effect is the same.

This looks like the other half of #2383. That issue was closed when ParamSpec support landed, and the argument is indeed accepted now — but the return type is still wrong.

Impact: we evaluated ty on a ~1600-file codebase that is clean under mypy strict. This one pattern produces 437 of 689 diagnostics, because our database accessors are overloaded on a `Literal[bool]` flag that selects the return type, and they are usually called through `executor.submit`.

Possibly related: #2568, #3415, #2799.

### Summary

ty models Pydantic constructors with lax coercion, so both of these pass:

```py
import pydantic

class Model(pydantic.BaseModel):
    count: int

Model(count='123')  # ty: ok — coerces to 123 at runtime
Model(count='abc')  # ty: ok — but raises ValidationError at runtime
```

The first is correct by the book. The second is the problem: ty accepts a call that always fails at runtime, because `str` is a valid lax input for `int` in general but this particular `str` is not.

`pydantic.mypy` with `init_typed = True` rejects both:

```
error: Argument "count" to "Model" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int"  [arg-type]
```

Teams that set `init_typed = True` have deliberately opted out of relying on coercion — they want declared field types enforced at construction. There is currently no way to express that in ty, which blocks migrating any codebase using this setting.

Request: an opt-in rule, off by default, that checks constructor arguments against the declared field types rather than the lax input types.

This is the same shape as #3966, where ty correctly honored `extra=ignore` but teams wanted the stricter check regardless, and the resolution was a rule they could turn off. The default would be reversed here: off by default, enabled by teams coming from `init_typed = True`.

### Version

body_text:
When a generic calll is inferred against a union type context, we narrow to the first union element to which the inferred type is assignable. However, an inference attempt that produces diagnostics may be considered assignable due to a fallback type of `Unknown`, despite another union element being more compatible.

```py
from typing import Callable

def f[T](x: T) -> list[T]:
    return [x]

f: list[Callable[[int], int]] | list[Callable[[str], str]] = f(lambda x: x.upper())
```

This can also happen during collection literal inference:

```py
f: list[Callable[[int], int]] | list[Callable[[str], str]] = [
    lambda x: x.upper(),  # error: [unresolved-attribute]
]
```

### Summary

If for whatever reason the process of the playground's inlay hints getting updated is slow/delayed, making an edit to the file then quickly inserting an inlay hint can cause that insertion to happen on the new data using the old ranges, making a mess.

For example, this code causes the inlay hint updating to happen extremely slowly:
https://play.ty.dev/1e846ab5-398e-42c4-b84e-e2c71e2bcfc3
```py
A: A = 1

a = (A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A)

x = [1]
```
In that code, `x` has an inlay hint of `: list[int]`. If you open the link/reload the page, wait for inlay hints to load, add a newline above the `x = [1]`, and then quickly insert `x`'s inlay hint, you end up with this:
```py
A: A = 1

a = (A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A, A)

: list[int]
x = [1]
```
Where the inlay hint got placed in the wrong place.
If you mess around with this enough, you can eventually get this error in the JS console:
```
Uncaught Error: Illegal value for lineNumber
```

body_text:
A shebang followed by a `# /// script` block is detected even when it is inside a string literal. The enclosing file is then resolved as a standalone PEP 723 script, so the project root drops out of the module search path and the file's own first-party imports fail.

This affects any file that embeds an example script in a string — test fixtures, code generators, docs builders.

## Repro

`pkg/lib.py`
```python
def helper() -> int:
    return 1
```

`pkg/user.py`
```python
from pkg.lib import helper

SCRIPT = '''#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# ///
'''
```

```console
$ ty check .
error[unresolved-import]: Cannot resolve imported module `pkg.lib`
 --> pkg/user.py:1:6
  |
1 | from pkg.lib import helper
  |      ^^^^^^^
info: Searched in the following paths during module resolution:
info:   1. vendored://stdlib (stdlib typeshed stubs vendored by ty)
info:   2. .venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages (site-packages)
```

The project root is absent from the search paths.

## Regression range

0.0.71 passes, 0.0.72 fails. Confirmed still failing on 0.0.73, 0.0.74, 0.0.75, 0.0.76, 0.0.79, 0.0.81, 0.0.82.

## Trigger requires both parts

| content inside the string | result |
|---|---|
| shebang only | clean |
| `# /// script` block only | clean |
| shebang + block | `unresolved-import` |

Any shebang works; it need not be `uv run --script`. An empty block (`# /// script` then `# ///`) is enough.

Independent of whether `__init__.py` is present, and of whether a `pyproject.toml` exists.

## Expected

PEP 723 detection should only consider comments at module level, not text inside string literals.

The enclosing file is then resolved as a standalone PEP 723 script, so the project root drops out of the module search path and the file's own first-party imports fail.

This affects any file that embeds an example script in a string — test fixtures, code generators, docs builders.

## Repro

`pkg/lib.py`
```python
def helper() -> int:
    return 1
```

`pkg/user.py`
```python
from pkg.lib import helper

SCRIPT = '''#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# ///
'''
```

error[unresolved-import]: Cannot resolve imported module `pkg.lib`
 --> pkg/user.py:1:6
  |
1 | from pkg.lib import helper
  |      ^^^^^^^
info: Searched in the following paths during module resolution:
info:   1. vendored://stdlib (stdlib typeshed stubs vendored by ty)
info:   2. .venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages (site-packages)
```

The project root is absent from the search paths.

## Regression range

0.0.71 passes, 0.0.72 fails. Confirmed still failing on 0.0.73, 0.0.74, 0.0.75, 0.0.76, 0.0.79, 0.0.81, 0.0.82.

## Trigger requires both parts

| content inside the string | result |
|---|---|
| shebang only | clean |
| `# /// script` block only | clean |
| shebang + block | `unresolved-import` |

Any shebang works; it need not be `uv run --script`. An empty block (`# /// script` then `# ///`) is enough.

Independent of whether `__init__.py` is present, and of whether a `pyproject.toml` exists.

## Expected

PEP 723 detection should only consider comments at module level, not text inside string literals.

### Summary

I have a bit of an odd issue with ty reporting an unknown attribute error when instantiating an `attrs` class that only comes up in very specific circumstances where a field has both an alias and a validator -- but only when the validator has a specific signature.

Here is the minimal reproducible example:

```python
# test.py
import attrs
from typing import Any

def validate_f2(inst: Any, attr: attrs.Attribute, value: str|None):
    if value is None or len(value) > 0:
        return

    raise ValueError("value must have a length if it is supplied")

@attrs.define
class A:
    _field1: str | None = attrs.field(alias="field1", default=None)
    _field2: str | None = attrs.field(alias="field2", default=None, validator=validate_f2)

a = A(field1="hi", field2="hello")
```

running `ty check test.py` produces the following output
```bash
error[unknown-argument]: Argument `field2` does not match any known parameter
  --> test.py:16:20
   |
16 | a = A(field1="hi", field2="hello")
   |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

BUT, if we change the signature on the validator so the `value` parameter has type `str` instead of `str|None`, i.e. to

```python
def validate_f2(inst: Any, attr: attrs.Attribute, value: str): ...
```

the check passes fine.  This shouldn't be necessary as the field is declared with `None` as a valid value. And in any event, if the issue were that the validator was accepting invalid values, I'd expect a different error message.

This issue is potentially marginally related to other requests for better `attrs` support, but it is not the same as any that I can see.  Specifically, it is NOT the same issue as #2474 or #1742 -- although the example uses private attributes, the alias in the example is declared explicitly--unlike what those two issues are asking for, which is an implicit alias. And explicit aliases ARE supported -- just not in this one very peculiar circumstance.

Any help would be appreciated.

### Summary

A concrete subclass assigns a callable to an instance attribute with the same name as a protocol method. ty 0.0.81 accepts this; ty 0.0.82 reports `call-non-callable` when constructing the subclass.

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Protocol

class Capybara(Protocol):
    def forage(self) -> None: ...

class Hutia(Capybara):
    forage: Callable[[], None]

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.forage = lambda: None

Hutia().forage()
```

Expected: no diagnostic. The assignment implements the protocol method, and `Hutia().forage()` executes successfully in Python.

Actual with 0.0.82:

```text
error[call-non-callable]: Cannot instantiate `Hutia` with unimplemented abstract method `forage`
```

0.0.81: `All checks passed!`

The same behavior occurs with an async protocol method and an `AsyncMock`-typed instance attribute assigned in `__init__`.

Possibly related to [#4552](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4552), but this example has no slots or abstract property. That issue is closed following a slots-specific fix.

> I just ran into what seems like the same or a very similar issue on a Linux machine with ~28 GB of RAM. When I open a single ~500 line Python file in nvim (0.12.5, built-in LSP client) in a large monorepo (~40,000 files of which ~7,000 are Python files), the ty server (0.0.82) consumes ~15 GB in ~36 seconds. However, if I run ty check on the same Python file, ty checks the file very quickly and exits cleanly. If I add an empty ty.toml file strategically to move the search root directory to reduce the number of files ty needs to examine, then the ty server's memory consumption is manageable.
> 
> ty check from the repo root also exhausts memory: with ulimit -v 8000000 it aborts with "memory allocation of 99518179 bytes failed" after a short run.
> https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4453#issuecomment-5737228478


> The answers to your questions are: (1) No, I had not typed anything. Memory starts climbing as soon as the file is opened and reaches >15 GB within ~36 s with no keystrokes. (2) Disabling completions.autoImport made no difference; the debug log confirms the server received auto_import: Some(false), and memory climbed at the same rate.
> 
> I dug a little further and found what may be the actual cause for my case on 0.0.82. Neovim's root detection put ty's project root at the .git root of a large shared scratch repo. That repo contains more than 14,000 .ipynb files totaling ~55 GB on disk (mostly embedded outputs) versus ~77 MB of .py files. I think the server reads and parses every notebook during its initial indexing pass, before checking the open file, and exhausts the memory. The attached debug log shows "Failed to read notebook" lines for files across many users' directories within the first 8 s (those particular files are LFS pointers or malformed; they're just evidence the server is reading notebooks repo-wide), followed by an allocation failure (SIGABRT).
> 
> [ty-server-redacted.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32488644/ty-server-redacted.log)
>

### Summary

Haven't found a matching issue when checking for overload + call. Apologies if already existing.

Calling a type `Foo` like `Foo(arg)` work without issues, but when the type is provided as a `Callable` argument to another function or method, it doesn't pick the right overload, resulting in erroneous outputs.

## Example

`Vec[T]` implement `collections::abc::MutableSequence[T]`, and `Seq[T]`,  spoilers ahead,  `collections::abc::Sequence[T]`.

Hence the former is/should be invariant, and the latter covariant.

Note that all the typing lives in stub. the source code comes from rust.

```python
import operator
from typing import assert_type

from pyochain import Option, Seq, Some, Vec


def check_constructor_call_context() -> None:
    """Constructors should be handled the same, regardless of the call context.

    Checking with `Seq` and `Vec` to ensure variance doesn't affect the result.

    Warning:
        Currently only passes with `basedpyright`
    """
    x = assert_type(Seq([1]), Seq[int])

    _vec_standard = assert_type(Vec(x), Vec[int])
    _seq_standard = assert_type(Seq(x), Seq[int])

    _vec_called = assert_type(operator.call(Vec, x), Vec[int])
    _seq_called = assert_type(operator.call(Seq, x), Seq[int])

    _vec_piped = assert_type(x.pipe(Vec), Vec[int])
    _seq_piped = assert_type(x.pipe(Seq), Seq[int])

    _seq_collected = assert_type(x.iter().collect(Seq), Seq[int])
    _vec_collected = assert_type(x.iter().collect(Vec), Vec[int])

    x_opt = assert_type(Some(x), Option[Seq[int]])
    _seq_mapped = assert_type(x_opt.map(Vec).unwrap(), Vec[int])
    _vec_mapped = assert_type(x_opt.map(Seq).unwrap(), Seq[int])
```

Both of them have thee exact same constructor signature:
```python
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, /) -> Self: ...
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, data: Iterable[T], /) -> Self: ...
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, data: T, /, *more: T) -> Self: ...
    def __new__(cls, data: Iterable[T] | T = (), /, *more: T) -> Self: """documentation"""
```

`pipe` uses `ParamSpec`, whilst `collect` doesn't. So it doesn't seem to be the cause.

Basedpyright report nothing, which is expected, while pyrefly seems to have the same issues as ty here.

File: https://github.com/OutSquareCapital/pyochain/blob/master/tests/test_typing/check_mixins.py

[`pipe` method](https://github.com/OutSquareCapital/pyochain/blob/43c237777225a861a9994df01321e3e6b35fa642/pyochain/abc/_mixins.pyi#L8)

[`collect` method](https://github.com/OutSquareCapital/pyochain/blob/43c237777225a861a9994df01321e3e6b35fa642/pyochain/abc/_iterator.pyi#L813)

[`ty.toml` config](https://github.com/OutSquareCapital/pyochain/blob/master/ty.toml)

## Command

at the repo root:

```shell
uvx ty check tests/test_typing/check_mixins.py
```

output:
```shell

  --> tests\test_typing\check_mixins.py:20:19

info: `Seq[int]` and `Seq[T@Seq]` are not equivalent types

  --> tests\test_typing\check_mixins.py:23:18

   |                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^-----------^^^^^^^^^^^

Haven't found a matching issue when checking for overload + call. Apologies if already existing.

Calling a type `Foo` like `Foo(arg)` work without issues, but when the type is provided as a `Callable` argument to another function or method, it doesn't pick the right overload, resulting in erroneous outputs.

## Example

`Vec[T]` implement `collections::abc::MutableSequence[T]`, and `Seq[T]`,  spoilers ahead,  `collections::abc::Sequence[T]`.

Hence the former is/should be invariant, and the latter covariant.

Note that all the typing lives in stub. the source code comes from rust.

```python
import operator
from typing import assert_type

from pyochain import Option, Seq, Some, Vec


def check_constructor_call_context() -> None:
    """Constructors should be handled the same, regardless of the call context.

    Checking with `Seq` and `Vec` to ensure variance doesn't affect the result.

    Warning:
        Currently only passes with `basedpyright`
    """
    x = assert_type(Seq([1]), Seq[int])

    _vec_standard = assert_type(Vec(x), Vec[int])
    _seq_standard = assert_type(Seq(x), Seq[int])

    _vec_called = assert_type(operator.call(Vec, x), Vec[int])
    _seq_called = assert_type(operator.call(Seq, x), Seq[int])

    _vec_piped = assert_type(x.pipe(Vec), Vec[int])
    _seq_piped = assert_type(x.pipe(Seq), Seq[int])

    _seq_collected = assert_type(x.iter().collect(Seq), Seq[int])
    _vec_collected = assert_type(x.iter().collect(Vec), Vec[int])

    x_opt = assert_type(Some(x), Option[Seq[int]])
    _seq_mapped = assert_type(x_opt.map(Vec).unwrap(), Vec[int])
    _vec_mapped = assert_type(x_opt.map(Seq).unwrap(), Seq[int])
```

Both of them have thee exact same constructor signature:
```python
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, /) -> Self: ...
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, data: Iterable[T], /) -> Self: ...
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, data: T, /, *more: T) -> Self: ...
    def __new__(cls, data: Iterable[T] | T = (), /, *more: T) -> Self: """documentation"""
```

`pipe` uses `ParamSpec`, whilst `collect` doesn't. So it doesn't seem to be the cause.

Basedpyright report nothing, which is expected, while pyrefly seems to have the same issues as ty here.

When inferring a constrained type variable from a fixed caller type variable, we may only preserve the caller type variable through the generic call if it is also constrained, and its constraints are a subset of the declared constraints of the callee (see https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/28814 for details). Notably, this means that if the caller's type variable has an upper bound as opposed to a subset of the declared constraints, it may not be preserved:

For example:

```py
def double[T: (int, str, bytes)](value: T) -> T:
    return value + value

def _[U: bool](value: U) -> U:
    reveal_type(double(value))  # revealed: int
    return double(value)  # error: [invalid-return-type]
```

However, we still incorrectly preserve a caller's type variable through a constrained type variable if it is declared with a gradual upper bound:

```py
def _[U: Any](value: U) -> None:
    # TODO: This is unsound, and should reveal Any.
    reveal_type(double(value))  # revealed: U@_
```

Fixing this behavior exposes a number of interesting cases involving gradual evidence that we don't handle correctly. For example, if there are no declared constraints which satisfy the call, we should prefer a gradual solution.

```py
def f[T: (int, str)](values: list[T]) -> list[T]: ...

def _[U: Any](values: list[U]):
    reveal_type(f(values))  # expected: list[Any]
```

If there is a single declared constraint which satisfies the call, we should instead prefer it over a gradual solution:

```py
def f[T: (list[int], str)](x: T) -> T:
    return x

def caller(x: list[Any]):
    reveal_type(f(x))  # expected: list[int]
```

A more tricky case involves multiple satisfying declared constraints as well as gradual evidence:

```py
def f[T: (tuple[int, int], tuple[int, str])](x: T) -> T:
    raise NotImplementedError

def caller(x: tuple[bool, Any]):
    reveal_type(f(x))  # expected: tuple[int, Any]
```

Here, we wish to preserve the graduality of the caller without choosing a specific declared constraint, i.e., to merge the inference evidence with the validity constraints. This should also apply when we have both static and gradual inference evidence from the caller (as opposed to our current `has_only_gradual_evidence` heuristic):

```py
from typing import Any, Callable

def f[T: (int, str)](x: T, consume: Callable[[T], None]) -> T:
    return x

def caller(x: Any, consume: Callable[[object], None]):
    reveal_type(f(x, consume))  # Currently: Any
```

### Summary

When accessing a submodule as an attribute on an imported package module in an expression (e.g., `pkg.submodule`), `textDocument/definition` on `submodule` returns `None`, even though:
1. `hover` on `submodule` correctly resolves it as `<module 'pkg.submodule'>`.
2. Go-to-definition on `submodule` in the import statement `import pkg.submodule` works.
3. Go-to-definition on `submodule` in `from pkg import submodule` works.

#### Minimal Reproduction

Project layout:
```
pkg/
  __init__.py    # empty
  sub.py         # dummy definition
main.py
```

`main.py`:
```python
import pkg.sub

# 1. Hover on `sub` correctly shows: <module 'pkg.sub'>
# 2. Go-to-definition on `sub` in `import pkg.sub` above navigates to `pkg/sub.py`
# 3. Go-to-definition on `sub` in the expression below returns None (no definition):
val = pkg.sub
```

**Expected behavior:**
Pressing Go to Definition on `sub` in `val = pkg.sub` should resolve to `pkg/sub.py` (or `pkg/sub/__init__.py`).

#### Relevant code in `ty_python_semantic`

In `crates/ty_python_semantic/src/types/definition_resolution.rs`:
- For import statements, `resolve_from_import_definitions` includes a fallback to `resolve_from_import_submodule_definitions` if symbol lookup in the package global scope returns empty.
- However, in `definitions_for_attribute`, when matching `Type::ModuleLiteral`:
```rust
if let Type::ModuleLiteral(module_literal) = ty {
    if let Some(module_file) = module_literal
        .module(db)
        .file(db)
        .map(|file| ProgramFile::new(db, file, env.program(db)))
    {
        let module_scope = global_scope(db, module_file);
        for def in find_symbol_in_scope(db, module_scope, name_str) {
            resolved.extend(resolve_definition(
                db,
                env,
                def,
                Some(name_str),
                ImportAliasResolution::ResolveAliases,
            ));
        }
    }
    continue;
}
```
If `name_str` is not explicitly bound in `module_scope` (i.e. not defined in `pkg/__init__.py`), `find_symbol_in_scope` yields no definitions, and the loop continues without checking whether `name_str` is an imported submodule of `module_literal`.

### Version

This seems to be related to gradual constraints, but it doesn't seem like #4536 describes this case, so I'm reporting it separately (FYI @ibraheemdev):

```py
from typing import Any, Callable

class C:
    def method(self: Any) -> None:
        pass

    def test(self) -> None:
        # Object of type `bound method Self@test.method() -> None` is not assignable to `() -> None`
        callback: Callable[[], None] = self.method
        callback()
```

When `Any` annotation is removed, or replaced with `Self` or `object`, the error goes away.

### Summary

After narrowing a TypeVar whose upper bound is a union, ty stops reporting attribute accesses that are only valid on some members of the bound. The same code using the union directly (no TypeVar) is correctly reported, as is the un-narrowed TypeVar.

```python
from typing import reveal_type


class A:
    y: int


class B: ...


def with_union(v: A | B) -> int:
    if isinstance(v, A):
        return 0
    return v.y  # error: Object of type `B & ~A` has no attribute `y`  ✅


def with_typevar[T: A | B](v: T) -> int:
    if isinstance(v, A):
        return 0
    reveal_type(v)  # T@with_typevar & ~A
    return v.y  # no error ❌


def positive_narrowing[T: A | B](v: T) -> int:
    if isinstance(v, B):
        reveal_type(v)  # T@positive_narrowing & B
        return v.y  # no error ❌
    return 0
```

Accessing an attribute that exists on no member of the bound (e.g. `v.does_not_exist`) is still reported, so it looks like attribute lookup on `T & X` doesn't distribute the union bound of `T` (e.g. `(A | B) & ~A → B & ~A`) and treats the attribute as available because it exists on one bound member. The same happens with legacy `TypeVar("T", bound=A | B)` and with `match` narrowing (`case A(): ... case _: v.y`). mypy reports all of these.

Command: `ty check repro.py`
Repro: https://play.ty.dev/6be32611-958b-4319-9fca-5267f7ece38a

The same happens with legacy `TypeVar("T", bound=A | B)` and with `match` narrowing (`case A(): ... case _: v.y`). mypy reports all of these.

A generic callable whose return type contains both an unconstrained outer type variable and an inferred type variable can be passed where its return type is bounded by `tuple[str, object]`. This lets code rely on the first element being a string even when it is an integer.

```python
from typing import Callable


def forward[U, R: tuple[str, object]](factory: Callable[[U], R], arg: U) -> R:
    result = factory(arg)
    result[0].upper()
    return result


def outer[S](value: S) -> None:
    def factory[U](arg: U) -> tuple[S, U]:
        return value, arg

    forward(factory, 1)


outer(1)
```

`ty check --python-version 3.12 repro.py` reports `All checks passed!`, but running the example raises `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'upper'`. The call to `forward` should be rejected because `S` is not bounded by `str`, even though `U` can be inferred from the argument.

Tested with ty built from Ruff main commit `ccaed68b562c2c2eeed78395f34be1828c62b885`.

ty’s integrated notebook support is already very useful: it allows checking notebooks directly from the CLI without conversion or wrapper tools. Accounting for Jupyter’s import behavior would make it even more useful in workspaces containing several independent notebook directories.

Consider this layout:

```text
project/
├── pyproject.toml
└── research/
    ├── strategy-a/
    │   ├── analysis.ipynb
    │   └── lib/
    │       └── studies.py
    └── strategy-b/
        ├── analysis.ipynb
        └── lib/
            └── studies.py
```

Each notebook imports its own helper module:

```python
from lib.studies import average_returns
```

This works when the Jupyter kernel runs from the notebook’s directory, and Pylance resolves the import in VS Code. However, running `ty check research/` from the project root reports `unresolved-import`.

Adding `--extra-search-path research/strategy-a` resolves the error when checking that directory alone. But this is not a general solution for a workspace-wide check: adding both directories creates shared search paths, leaving the two distinct `lib.studies` modules ambiguous.

Could ty resolve these imports relative to **each notebook’s containing directory**, or provide a notebook-specific setting for this behavior? Ideally, a single `ty check research/` would resolve each notebook’s helpers independently.

Related: #1297 concerns another aspect of notebook namespaces—IPython-provided names such as `display`. This request concerns module search paths rather than injected builtins.

In the example below, the conflicting arguments `a` and `b` cause the constraint solver to collapse the entire solutions path to unsatisfiable. This means that we end up suppressing diagnostics for the unrelated type variable, `T`, whose constraints were not satisfied:

```py
def f[T: (int, str), U](
    x: T, y: T, a: list[U], b: list[U]
) -> T:
    return x

def _(x: int, y: str, a: list[int], b: list[str]):
    # error[invalid-argument-type]: Argument to function `f` is incorrect: Expected `list[int | str]`, found `list[int]`
    # error[invalid-argument-type]: Argument to function `f` is incorrect: Expected `list[int | str]`, found `list[int]`
    f(x, y, a, b)
```

Similarly, we do not report unsatisfied constraints on the same type variable:
```py
def f[T: (int, str)](x: list[T], y: list[T]) -> T:
    return x[0]

def _(a: list[int], b: list[str]):
    # error[invalid-argument-type]: Argument to function `f` is incorrect: Expected `list[int | str]`, found `list[int]`
    # error[invalid-argument-type]: Argument to function `f` is incorrect: Expected `list[int | str]`, found `list[int]`
    f(a, b)
```

This example is less clear, as it leads to the question of how we want to handle reporting conflicting invariant bounds in the first place. We currently fallback to the union of all inferred bounds, which means we end up reporting a diagnostic as a result of the arguments not satisfying the chosen specialization -- despite the chosen specialization being invalid in the first place. Ideally these diagnostics would be reported by the constraint solver directly when encountering the unsatisfiable bounds, and we would not have the need for a recovery specialization at all.

The constraint solver intersects inferred gradual lower bounds with any upper bounds to restrict the range of the gradual solution. However, we currently top-materialize the upper bounds, which can lose intended graduality and lead to false positives:

```py
from _typeshed import SupportsNext
from typing import Any, Callable, reveal_type

def infer[T](value: T, consumer: Callable[[T], None]) -> T:
    return value

def _(
    value: Any,
    consumer: Callable[[SupportsNext[Any]], None],
) -> None:
    # TODO: This should be `SupportsNext[Any]`.
    iterator = reveal_type(infer(value, consumer)) # revealed: SupportsNext[object] & Any
    reveal_type(next(iterator))  # revealed: object
```

The same limitation applies to declared upper bounds:

```py
def infer[T: SupportsNext[Any]](value: Callable[[T], None]) -> T:
    raise NotImplementedError

def _(
    value: Callable[[Any], None]
) -> None:
    # TODO: This should be `SupportsNext[Any]`.
    iterator = reveal_type(infer(value)) # revealed: Any & SupportsNext[object]
    reveal_type(next(iterator))  # revealed: object
```

body_text:
When typing `def ` (or `def __`) inside a class body, the ty language server doesn't offer completions for methods to override from parent classes, nor for common magic methods. Pylance offers these as completions and inserts the full signature with typing.


```python
class Base:
    def process(self, data: bytes, *, strict: bool = False) -> str: ...

class Vector(Base):
    def 
```

Suggest: process that produces:
```python
def process(self, data: bytes, *, strict: bool = False) -> str:
```

The same applies to magic methods, `__len__`, `__str__` etc.

Why it's useful ?
- Avoids having to recheck definition and copy it again
- Avoids using wrong arguments names
- Speeds up overrides

Approaches:
- Show standards magic methods for all classes: `__repr__`, `__eq__` etc. [Incomplete list
](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#special-method-names)
- Then for each parent class, narrow down if the parent implements it and also add all of the parent methods.

### Summary

`ty` reports an `invalid-return-type` diagnostic when class patterns cover all values of an attribute's annotated type. It reports that the function can implicitly return `None`, even though each case returns.

### Reproduction

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Box:
    value: int | str


def describe(box: Box) -> str:
    match box:
        case Box(value=int()):
            return "int"
        case Box(value=str()):
            return "str"
```

With ty 0.0.84 and `--python-version 3.12`, this produces:

```text
error[invalid-return-type]: Function can implicitly return `None`, which is not assignable to return type `str`
```

### Expected behavior

The two cases cover both declared types of `value`. If we assume the attribute is present and its value stays the same while the cases are evaluated, ty should consider the match exhaustive and not report an implicit return.

### Examples from the ecosystem

The [ecosystem report for ruff#29053](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29053#issuecomment-5936236342) flagged these matches with the proposed `non-exhaustive-match` rule, as an error in pyochain. The two Expression examples also produced implicit-return diagnostics in a local comparison. Unlike the reproduction above, these examples match literal values inside the class patterns; pyochain uses positional patterns for `Some.value`.

- **Expression**, `docs/guides/domain-modeling.py`: [28](https://github.com/cognitedata/Expression/blob/257e3a77f90a14056c405db66af302625827e05b/docs/guides/domain-modeling.py#L28).
- **Expression**, `docs/tutorial/data_modelling.py`: [45](https://github.com/cognitedata/Expression/blob/257e3a77f90a14056c405db66af302625827e05b/docs/tutorial/data_modelling.py#L45).
- **pyochain**, `tests/test_typing/check_options.py`: [40](https://github.com/OutSquareCapital/pyochain/blob/41039f9ee1070c61d14b0d9f4323cc7d38d10d71/tests/test_typing/check_options.py#L40).

### Summary

When a method annotates `self` with a `TypeVarTuple`-prefixed specialization of its class (`self: "C[V, Unpack[Q]]"`), ty does not solve `V` and `Q` from the receiver when it binds the method. The bound method stays generic, so `V` is then inferred from the call arguments alone, and the result is checked back against the receiver. The same pattern with a plain `TypeVar` (`self: "C[V]"`) binds as expected.

```python
from typing import Any, Callable, Generic, TypeVar, TypeVarTuple, Unpack, reveal_type

P = TypeVarTuple("P")
Q = TypeVarTuple("Q")
T = TypeVar("T")
V = TypeVar("V")


class Prefixed(Generic[Unpack[P]]):
    def __call__(self: "Prefixed[V, Unpack[Q]]", value: V) -> "Prefixed[Unpack[Q]]": ...


class Single(Generic[T]):
    def __call__(self: "Single[V]", value: V) -> V: ...


class Var(Generic[T]): ...


class Handler(Generic[Unpack[P]]):
    def __call__(self: "Handler[V, Unpack[Q]]", value: V | Var[V]) -> "Handler[Unpack[Q]]": ...


def f(p: Prefixed[int, str], s: Single[int], h: Handler[int], v: Var[int]) -> None:
    reveal_type(p.__call__)
    reveal_type(s.__call__)
    p("x")
    h(v)
    c: Callable[[int], Any] = p
```

ty 0.0.84 (and main at cbc71c28d):

```
25:17: info[revealed-type] Revealed type: `bound method Prefixed[int, str].__call__[V, *Q](value: V) -> Prefixed[*tuple[*Q]]`
26:17: info[revealed-type] Revealed type: `bound method Single[int].__call__(value: int) -> int`
27:5: error[invalid-argument-type] Argument to bound method `Prefixed.__call__` is incorrect: Expected `Prefixed[int | Literal["x"], str]`, found `Prefixed[int, str]`
28:5: error[invalid-argument-type] Argument to bound method `Handler.__call__` is incorrect: Expected `Handler[int | Var[int]]`, found `Handler[int]`
29:31: error[invalid-assignment] Object of type `Prefixed[int, str]` is not assignable to `(int, /) -> Any`
```

Expected (this is what pyright 1.1.414 reports):

- `p.__call__` is `(value: int) -> Prefixed[str]`, like `s.__call__` is `(value: int) -> int`.
- `p("x")` is an error because `str` is not assignable to `int`, not because the receiver would have to be `Prefixed[int | Literal["x"], str]`.
- `h(v)` is fine: `V` is `int` from the receiver, and `Var[int]` is assignable to `int | Var[int]`.
- `Prefixed[int, str]` is assignable to `Callable[[int], Any]`.

### Impact

This is the shape of Reflex's `EventCallback`, whose `__call__` overloads are written as `self: "EventCallback[V, Unpack[Q]]", value: V | Var[V]`. In a Reflex app every call of an event handler with a frontend value, e.g. `on_click=State.select(item.id)`, is reported as `invalid-argument-type`, and no event handler is assignable to a `Callable` type that accepts its arguments.

The repro is clean on 0.0.60, where `Prefixed` was still `@Todo`, and fails from 0.0.61 on, i.e. since `TypeVarTuple` support landed. Possibly related to #4152.

body_text:
In astral-sh/ruff#24240 I added glob support to `environment.extra-paths`. @MichaReiser pointed out that the monorepo case should be in the root setting and that he would be fine with adding that feature so I closed that PR. I want to start that work, for `environment.root` but first I want to confirm that this is still desired before I begin.

The use case is a monorepo where every package has the same layout:

```toml
[tool.ty.environment]
root = ["./packages/*/src"]
```

instead of listing each package's `src` directory by hand. #179 originally asked
for this, but it was closed when `root` became a list.


What I'm planning:

- Use the PEP 639 portable glob syntax for `src.include` and `src.exclude`.
- Entries that don't have any glob characters work just like they do now.
- All patterns are expanded during one directory walk. This lets us skip directories that can't possibly match as mentioned in the review of #24240.
- Since `root` is processed in priority order the matches, for each pattern are. Placed exactly where the pattern appears in the list.
- Patterns will not support `~` or environment variable expansion.


Two things I would like your opinion on:

1. A literal root that does not exist is an error today. Should a pattern that matches no directory be a warning or an error?
2. I would expand the patterns when the program settings are resolved. In the editor that means a created matching directory is not picked up until the configuration changes. Is that acceptable, for the version?

### Summary

A dict literal keyed by a `TypeVar` object is inferred as a `dict` whose key type is not the nominal `TypeVar` class, so it is not assignable to `Mapping[TypeVar, ...]` even though both are displayed as `TypeVar`. With type context (a declared variable, or the literal passed straight to the call) it is accepted, and a literal key such as `1` is widened to `int` as expected.

```python
from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Any, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T", bound=int)


def takes(m: Mapping[TypeVar, Any]) -> None: ...


def inferred(model: type[T]) -> None:
    d = {T: model}
    takes(d)  # error


def with_context(model: type[T]) -> None:
    takes({T: model})  # fine


def annotated(model: type[T]) -> None:
    d: dict[TypeVar, Any] = {T: model}
    takes(d)  # fine


def int_keys(model: type[T]) -> None:
    def takes_int(m: Mapping[int, Any]) -> None: ...

    d = {1: model}
    takes_int(d)  # fine: the literal key is widened to `int`
```

ty 0.0.84, and main at 127e77ef8 (2026-10-02):

```
13:11: error[invalid-argument-type] Argument to function `takes` is incorrect: Expected `Mapping[TypeVar, Any]`, found `dict[TypeVar, type[T@inferred]]`
```

Expected: no diagnostic. The key of `{T: model}` should be widened to `TypeVar` the way `{1: ...}` gets an `int` key, since `Mapping` (like `dict`) is invariant in its key type. pyright 1.1.414 accepts the file, and reveals `d` as `dict[TypeVar, type[T@inferred]]` as well.

The diagnostic is also hard to act on: the expected and found key types are both printed as `TypeVar`, so nothing in the message points at the key.

### Context

This came up in code that maps a generic class's type parameters to their runtime arguments (`{SQLAModel: model}`) and passes the map to a helper that takes `Mapping[TypeVar, ...]`.

### Version

body_text:
ty treats an enum as potentially having additional members when it has a custom metaclass that overrides `__new__` or `__prepare__`. As a result, ty does not consider a match over every declared member exhaustive, even when the metaclass simply delegates to `EnumMeta`:

```python
from enum import Enum, EnumMeta

class Meta(EnumMeta):
    def __new__(cls, name, bases, namespace):
        return super().__new__(cls, name, bases, namespace)

class Color(Enum, metaclass=Meta):
    RED = 1
    BLUE = 2

def describe(value: Color) -> str:  # error: [invalid-return-type] "Can implicitly return `None`"
    match value:
        case Color.RED:
            return "red"
        case Color.BLUE:
            return "blue"
```

As well as the false-positive `invalid-return-type` diagnostic on `describe` here, the proposed [`non-exhaustive-match` rule](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29053) also reports this match as non-exhaustive.

I think it might be more pragmatic just to optimistically assume that the declared members of a non-`Flag` enum with members exhaust its possible values, even if this technically might not be the case for _all_ of these enums? The [typing specification’s enum literal expansion section](https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/enums.html#enum-literal-expansion) describes treating most enum types as the union of their literal members, with an exception for flags.

We made a similar pragmatic choice in [#27700](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27700), where we started treating enums with a custom `_missing_` method as exhaustive even though `_missing_` can create additional enum instances.

## Ecosystem examples

- rotki’s [`ProtocolsWithCache` match](https://github.com/rotki/rotki/blob/a0fc8a5a0e41c02fa6559e0386155201b1f08cb9/rotkehlchen/api/services/assets.py#L1078) and [`ZKSyncLiteTXType` match](https://github.com/rotki/rotki/blob/a0fc8a5a0e41c02fa6559e0386155201b1f08cb9/rotkehlchen/chain/zksync_lite/manager.py#L862) cover every declared member. Their [metaclass](https://github.com/rotki/rotki/blob/a0fc8a5a0e41c02fa6559e0386155201b1f08cb9/rotkehlchen/utils/mixins/enums.py#L10-L26) delegates enum construction to `EnumMeta` and does not add members.
- steam.py’s [`BucketType.get_bucket` match](https://github.com/Gobot1234/steam.py/blob/be70d6b7738eabdab3ba74969ddc36920cdf6cc1/steam/ext/commands/cooldown.py#L60) also covers every declared member, but ty reports that the method can implicitly return `None`. `BucketType` uses the project’s [custom enum implementation](https://github.com/Gobot1234/steam.py/blob/be70d6b7738eabdab3ba74969ddc36920cdf6cc1/steam/enums.py#L106), whose metaclass overrides enum construction.
- rotki’s [accounting import match](https://github.com/rotki/rotki/blob/a0fc8a5a0e41c02fa6559e0386155201b1f08cb9/rotkehlchen/accounting/debugimporter/json.py#L60) omits the declared `STAKING` member. Treating the enum as a union would allow the proposed rule to identify the missing member.

## Tradeoff

A custom metaclass can change the set of enum members, and code can also construct additional enum instances after the enum is created. Either can cause this assumption to miss values that exist at runtime. For example, steam.py’s enum implementation provides a [`try_value` method](https://github.com/Gobot1234/steam.py/blob/be70d6b7738eabdab3ba74969ddc36920cdf6cc1/steam/enums.py#L223-L228) that can create an instance for an unrecognized value. A `BucketType` created this way can fall through the match in `get_bucket`, even though ty would treat the match as exhaustive under this proposal.

## Ecosystem survey

Codex did an analysis of 511 distinct Python files returned by grep.app searches for [`(EnumMeta`](https://grep.app/search?f.lang=Python&q=%28EnumMeta), [`(enum.EnumMeta`](https://grep.app/search?f.lang=Python&q=%28enum.EnumMeta), [`(EnumType):`](https://grep.app/search?f.lang=Python&q=%28EnumType%29%3A), and [`(enum.EnumType`](https://grep.app/search?f.lang=Python&q=%28enum.EnumType). After excluding tests, vendored or copied third-party code, and clearly irrelevant or flag-only examples, the sample contained 67 metaclass definitions with their own `__new__` or `__prepare__`:

| Behaviour found in the inspected code | Metaclass definitions | Percentage |
|---|---:|---:|
| Creates additional members during class creation | **7** | **10.4%** |
| Otherwise, provides a way to add named members later | **3** | **4.5%** |
| Otherwise, an associated `_missing_` method creates unregistered instances | **3** | **4.5%** |
| No additional member creation found | **54** | **80.6%** |

Each definition is counted once, in the first applicable row. The first row includes one metaclass that turns a nested class declaration into a member; the other six add member names not declared in the enum body.

For example, [sentinelhub](https://github.com/sentinel-hub/sentinelhub-py/blob/e6c3694380af83f2e5a59dd5587d2a4b3c61e721/sentinelhub/constants.py#L70-L81) creates 120 members in its metaclass, while [python-cstruct](https://github.com/andreax79/python-cstruct/blob/fde9641c3f7bf716dc11882c90d4d5e4832be3ad/cstruct/abstract.py#L311-L336) creates members from a C enum declaration. [agentscope-runtime](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope-runtime/blob/22072fd7075ce0c6f43cb39509d6a14b0e60ddb5/src/agentscope_runtime/sandbox/enums.py#L19-L45) instead provides an API to add members later. By contrast, [Django’s choices metaclass](https://github.com/django/django/blob/a461af8ce48762d7ec602260aaff81014ddccbcb/django/db/models/enums.py#L10-L33) only transforms already-declared members.

<details>
<summary>Ecosystem survey details</summary>

The searches are ranked rather than random and miss aliases and indirect subclasses. The inspection also cannot rule out additional behaviour in uninspected subclasses or helpers. The counts are of metaclass definitions: a definition may be used by many enums or may not be used at all. Some hooks are conditional and may not trigger ty’s check in every configuration.

Nine definitions are copies of one generated SDK implementation that did not create extra members in the inspected code; counting that group once gives 7 of 59 for class-creation injection. This is not a complete deduplication. A stub can also declare a dynamically added member, so the seven are not necessarily seven cases where ty would miss a member.

### Survey classifications

The definitions below are grouped using the same precedence as the summary table. The links point to revisions whose files match those inspected for the survey.

#### Additional members during class creation (7)

- [`andreax79/python-cstruct` — `CEnumMeta`](https://github.com/andreax79/python-cstruct/blob/fde9641c3f7bf716dc11882c90d4d5e4832be3ad/cstruct/abstract.py#L311): Its prepared namespace parses C enum declarations and inserts their constants as members.
- [`pythongssapi/python-gssapi` — `ExtendableEnum`](https://github.com/pythongssapi/python-gssapi/blob/32aeef9756effd18d44e6e34ae211a7df7ce1214/gssapi/raw/_enum_extensions/__init__.py#L18): Adds names from an extension registry during class creation.

{"repository": "astral-sh/ty", "task_candidate_id": 1796, "repository_id": 38, "issue_number": 4662, "github_issue_id": 5699337601, "html_url": "https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4662", "created_at": "2026-10-04T12:36:10+00:00", "author_association": "MEMBER", "title": "Consider treating enums with custom metaclasses as exhaustive", "body_text": "ty treats an enum as potentially having additional members when it has a custom metaclass that overrides `__new__` or `__prepare__`. As a result, ty does not consider a match over every declared member exhaustive, even when the metaclass simply delegates to `EnumMeta`:

```python
from enum import Enum, EnumMeta

class Meta(EnumMeta):
    def __new__(cls, name, bases, namespace):
        return super().__new__(cls, name, bases, namespace)

class Color(Enum, metaclass=Meta):
    RED = 1
    BLUE = 2

def describe(value: Color) -> str:  # error: [invalid-return-type] "Can implicitly return `None`"
    match value:
        case Color.RED:
            return "red"
        case Color.BLUE:
            return "blue"
```

As well as the false-positive `invalid-return-type` diagnostic on `describe` here, the proposed [`non-exhaustive-match` rule](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/29053) also reports this match as non-exhaustive.

I think it might be more pragmatic just to optimistically assume that the declared members of a non-`Flag` enum with members exhaust its possible values, even if this technically might not be the case for _all_ of these enums? The [typing specification’s enum literal expansion section](https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/enums.html#enum-literal-expansion) describes treating most enum types as the union of their literal members, with an exception for flags.

We made a similar pragmatic choice in [#27700](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27700), where we started treating enums with a custom `_missing_` method as exhaustive even though `_missing_` can create additional enum instances.

## Ecosystem examples

- rotki’s [`ProtocolsWithCache` match](https://github.com/rotki/rotki/blob/a0fc8a5a0e41c02fa6559e0386155201b1f08cb9/rotkehlchen/api/services/assets.py#L1078) and [`ZKSyncLiteTXType` match](https://github.com/rotki/rotki/blob/a0fc8a5a0e41c02fa6559e0386155201b1f08cb9/rotkehlchen/chain/zksync_lite/manager.py#L862) cover every declared member. Their [metaclass](https://github.com/rotki/rotki/blob/a0fc8a5a0e41c02fa6559e0386155201b1f08cb9/rotkehlchen/utils/mixins/enums.py#L10-L26) delegates enum construction to `EnumMeta` and does not add members.
- steam.py’s [`BucketType.get_bucket` match](https://github.com/Gobot1234/steam.py/blob/be70d6b7738eabdab3ba74969ddc36920cdf6cc1/steam/ext/commands/cooldown.py#L60) also covers every declared member, but ty reports that the method can implicitly return `None`. `BucketType` uses the project’s [custom enum implementation](https://github.com/Gobot1234/steam.py/blob/be70d6b7738eabdab3ba74969ddc36920cdf6cc1/steam/enums.py#L106), whose metaclass overrides enum construction.
- rotki’s [accounting import match](https://github.com/rotki/rotki/blob/a0fc8a5a0e41c02fa6559e0386155201b1f08cb9/rotkehlchen/accounting/debugimporter/json.py#L60) omits the declared `STAKING` member. Treating the enum as a union would allow the proposed rule to identify the missing member.

## Tradeoff

A custom metaclass can change the set of enum members, and code can also construct additional enum instances after the enum is created. Either can cause this assumption to miss values that exist at runtime. For example, steam.py’s enum implementation provides a [`try_value` method](https://github.com/Gobot1234/steam.py/blob/be70d6b7738eabdab3ba74969ddc36920cdf6cc1/steam/enums.py#L223-L228) that can create an instance for an unrecognized value. A `BucketType` created this way can fall through the match in `get_bucket`, even though ty would treat the match as exhaustive under this proposal.

## Ecosystem survey

Codex did an analysis of 511 distinct Python files returned by grep.app searches for [`(EnumMeta`](https://grep.app/search?f.lang=Python&q=%28EnumMeta), [`(enum.EnumMeta`](https://grep.app/search?f.lang=Python&q=%28enum.EnumMeta), [`(EnumType):`](https://grep.app/search?f.lang=Python&q=%28EnumType%29%3A), and [`(enum.EnumType`](https://grep.app/search?f.lang=Python&q=%28enum.EnumType). After excluding tests, vendored or copied third-party code, and clearly irrelevant or flag-only examples, the sample contained 67 metaclass definitions with their own `__new__` or `__prepare__`:

| Behaviour found in the inspected code | Metaclass definitions | Percentage |
|---|---:|---:|
| Creates additional members during class creation | **7** | **10.4%** |
| Otherwise, provides a way to add named members later | **3** | **4.5%** |
| Otherwise, an associated `_missing_` method creates unregistered instances | **3** | **4.5%** |
| No additional member creation found | **54** | **80.6%** |

Each definition is counted once, in the first applicable row. The first row includes one metaclass that turns a nested class declaration into a member; the other six add member names not declared in the enum body.

For example, [sentinelhub](https://github.com/sentinel-hub/sentinelhub-py/blob/e6c3694380af83f2e5a59dd5587d2a4b3c61e721/sentinelhub/constants.py#L70-L81) creates 120 members in its metaclass, while [python-cstruct](https://github.com/andreax79/python-cstruct/blob/fde9641c3f7bf716dc11882c90d4d5e4832be3ad/cstruct/abstract.py#L311-L336) creates members from a C enum declaration. [agentscope-runtime](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope-runtime/blob/22072fd7075ce0c6f43cb39509d6a14b0e60ddb5/src/agentscope_runtime/sandbox/enums.py#L19-L45) instead provides an API to add members later. By contrast, [Django’s choices metaclass](https://github.com/django/django/blob/a461af8ce48762d7ec602260aaff81014ddccbcb/django/db/models/enums.py#L10-L33) only transforms already-declared members.

The searches are ranked rather than random and miss aliases and indirect subclasses. The inspection also cannot rule out additional behaviour in uninspected subclasses or helpers. The counts are of metaclass definitions: a definition may be used by many enums or may not be used at all. Some hooks are conditional and may not trigger ty’s check in every configuration.

Nine definitions are copies of one generated SDK implementation that did not create extra members in the inspected code; counting that group once gives 7 of 59 for class-creation injection. This is not a complete deduplication. A stub can also declare a dynamically added member, so the seven are not necessarily seven cases where ty would miss a member.

This is not very user friendly especially for people less in the weeds of python typing (who might be confused about `Never` type).

body_text:
### Summary

In lax mode, ty replaces the type arguments of a nested generic model with `Unknown` in the synthesized `__init__`. A field declared as `inner: Inner[T]` therefore accepts an `Inner` with the wrong type argument, even when Pydantic always rejects it at runtime. A plain field `value: T` is checked, and so is the nested field when the model sets `strict=True`.

```py
from typing import Generic, Literal, TypeVar

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

T = TypeVar("T")


class Inner(BaseModel, Generic[T]):
    value: T


class Outer(BaseModel, Generic[T]):
    inner: Inner[T]


class StrictOuter(BaseModel, Generic[T]):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)
    inner: Inner[T]


AB = Literal["a", "b"]

Inner[AB](value="c")  # error: Expected `Literal["a", "b"]`, found `Literal["c"]`
Outer[AB](inner=Inner[Literal["c"]](value="c"))  # no error
StrictOuter[AB](inner=Inner[Literal["c"]](value="c"))  # error: Expected `Inner[Literal["a", "b"]]`, found `Inner[Literal["c"]]`

reveal_type(Outer[AB].__init__)
# (self: Outer[Literal["a", "b"]], *, inner: Inner[Unknown] | Mapping[str, Any], **extra: Any) -> None
reveal_type(StrictOuter[AB].__init__)
# (self: StrictOuter[Literal["a", "b"]], *, inner: Inner[Literal["a", "b"]], **extra: Any) -> None
```

At runtime, all three calls raise `ValidationError: Input should be 'a' or 'b'`, because Pydantic re-validates an `Inner` instance of any parametrization against `Inner[AB]`. Pyright reports all three.

I'd expect the `Outer` call to be reported as well. Since Pydantic re-validates the instance, one option is to check the type argument covariantly against the lax input type of `T`. That works the same way as for the plain field `value: T`: `Inner[Literal["a"]]` stays accepted (and it does pass at runtime), while `Inner[Literal["c"]]` is rejected.

A related case: `Outer[AB](inner=Inner(value="c"))`, the more common way to write this, isn't reported even with `StrictOuter`. ty infers `Inner(value="c")` as `Inner[Unknown]`; it infers the type argument neither from the argument nor from the expected type. I can open a separate issue for that if you prefer.

Context: in [flodym](https://github.com/pik-piam/flodym) we use a `Literal` type parameter for the dimension letters, so that `DimensionSet[Literal["t", "e"]](dim_list=[Dimension(letter="w", ...)])` gets reported. That needs both of the cases above.

Related: #4540

### Version
