I work in a team with private repositories. Some of these repositories are used to develop python packages, which in turn are to be installed in other private python repositories used as services.

Some of the package repositories involve bindings from other languages like Rust. In the service repositories, we set up docker images, which we try to keep as small as possible. In particular, in order to not have to set up rust (even temporarily) in a python docker image, it is desirable to install our first party python packages via their wheels.

In the package repositories, the `.whl` files are assets uploaded to each tagged release and can be accessed by certain _browser urls_, which in turn can be written in our pyproject.toml files. The issue is that authorisations due to url forwarding (explained below).

## The setup ##

My system:

- `uv` v0.11.6
- `python` v3.14
- `osx`

### Repo A: Package ###

The "package" repository has (roughly) the following structure

```text
# https://github.com/<OWNER>/repo-a
|
|__ rust
|  |___ ( code base in rust with python bindings )
|  |___ Cargo.toml
|  |___ pyproject.toml (build back uses maturin)
|
|__ src
|  |__ /my-package
|
|__ pyproject.toml (includes subfolder ./rust as a workspace)
```

+ CI/CD pipelines that upload `.whl` files to the releases.

### Repo B: Service ###

The application repository has roughly the following setup

```text
|
|__ src
|  |__ ...
|
|__ pyproject.toml
|__ Dockerfile          (here we only wish to use slim python images without rust)
|__ docker-compose.yaml
```

+ CI/CD pipelines to build small docker images which get pushed to a registry.

Here `pyproject.toml` contains

```toml
...
dependencies = [
   ...
   "my-package @ https://github.com/<OWNER>/repo-a/releases/download/v1.0.0/my_package-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl",
   "my-package-rust @ https://github.com/<OWNER>/repo-a/releases/download/v1.0.0/my_package_rust-1.0.0-cp314-abi3-manylinux_2_34_x86_64.whl",
   ...
]
...
```

## GitHub + UV ##

I have a PAT set up with sufficient rights, and on my local machine, using

```bash
uv auth login
```

I am able to authenticate my user.

## What works ##

1. If in Repo-B above, I instead set up `pyproject.toml` as

    ```toml
    ...
    dependencies = [
       ...
       "my-package[rust] @ git+https://github.com/<OWNER>/my-package.git@v1.0.0",
       ...
    ]
    ...
    ```

    the command `uv sync` work and installs the private package.
    Due to the maturin subpackage, my machine compiles the rust code and builds the bindings.

2. In cases where e.g. Rust is not on the local machine, I want a consumer of Repo-B to be able to build the python dependencies from pre-built wheels. If I make Repo-A public, then the first setup of `pyproject.toml` (in Repo-B) might work. However, this needs to work in the private case.

##  The problem ##

Using the `pyproject.toml` for Repo-B with the `.whl`-dependencies, despite authorisation via my PAT, I am not able to install the pre-built wheels.

```bash
$ uv sync
$ ...
$ DEBUG Found credentials in plaintext store for https://github.com/<OWNER>/repo-a/releases/download/v1.0.0/my_package-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
  × Failed to download `repo-a @ https://github.com/<OWNER>/repo-a/releases/download/v1.0.0/my_package-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl`
  ├─▶ Failed to fetch: `https://github.com/<OWNER>/repo-a/releases/download/v1.0.0/my_package-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl`
  ╰─▶ HTTP status client error (404 Not Found) for url
      (https://github.com/<OWNER>/repo-a/releases/download/v1.0.0/my_package-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl)

```

The cause of this problem can be found by simply attempting to `/GET` the GitHub assets with the authorisation token:

```bash
curl -sIL \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${GITHUB_PAT}" \
  https://github.com/<OWNER>/repo-a/releases/download/v1.0.0/my_package-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
```

This results in

```bash
HTTP/2 404

date: ......
content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
content-length: 0
vary: X-PJAX, X-PJAX-Container, Turbo-Visit, Turbo-Frame, X-Requested-With,Accept-Encoding, Accept, X-Requested-With
cache-control: no-cache
set-cookie: _octo=GH*.*.********.********; domain=github.com; path=/; expires=......; secure; SameSite=Lax
set-cookie: _gh_sess=*************************************************; path=/; secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
strict-transport-security: max-age=123456; includeSubdomains; preload
x-frame-options: deny
x-content-type-options: nosniff
x-xss-protection: 0
referrer-policy: origin-when-cross-origin, strict-origin-when-cross-origin
content-security-policy: default-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; connect-src 'self'; form-action 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; script-src 'self'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'
server: github.com
x-github-request-id: ****:****:****:****:****
```

What happens is: the _browser_ url is

```bash
https://github.com/<OWNER>/repo-a/releases/download/v1.0.0/my_package-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
```

but the _real_ url (where GitHub actually stores the asset) is

```bash
https://api.github.com/repos/<OWNER>/repo-a/releases/assets/{id}
```

and when one runs `uv sync`, then in the background the `/GET` request forwards to this. Crucially, the _authorisation header_ is not carried over in the transaction. Hence, even if I authorise `uv` for

```bash
https://api.github.com/repos/<OWNER>/repo-a/releases/assets
```

the `uv sync` command will still result in an 404 error.

## Proposed solution ###

GitHub's [REST API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/releases/assets?apiVersion=2026-03-10) provides a methods to obtain assets and their ids:

```bash
# list assets incl. <ID>s (response is a list of dictionaries)
curl -L \
  -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${GITHUB_PAT}" \
  -H "X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10" \
  'https://api.github.com/repos/<OWNER>/<repo>/releases/tags/<TAG>'

# request to load asset
curl -L \
  -H "Accept: application/octet-stream" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${GITHUB_PAT}" \
  -H "X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10" \
  'https://api.github.com/repos/<OWNER>/<repo>/releases/assets/<ID>' \
  -o <pathto/filename.whl>
```

It should be be possible for `uv sync`, when going through dependencies, to recognise GitHub urls, and if it sees them to try to use the above api methods (as well as an understanding of the choice of architecture in `pyproject.toml` or the local machine) to get the appropriate asset id, an then using this authorise the "forwarded" url to load the appropriate `.whl` file.

## Restrictions ##

> [!NOTE]
> I do not wish to set this up using pypi or JFrog, as we do not wish to unnecessarily expand our infrastructure or costs. I can see that this appears very doable using just GitHub + `uv`, provided a few small fixes are made.

body_text:
### Summary

When using a virtual environment created by `uv venv` (without `--system-site-packages`), Python cannot import the `gi` module even though the necessary system package (`python-gobject`) is fully installed via the system package manager (Arch Linux, `pacman`). This causes matplotlib to fall back to the non-interactive `Agg` backend, preventing any plot windows from appearing.

The core issue is that standard virtual environments isolate from system site‑packages. While this is correct for pure Python packages, it breaks commonly used GUI libraries (GTK, Qt, Tk) that are often installed at the system level.

Current workarounds (`--system-site-packages`, manually compiling `PyGObject` in every project, `.pth` files) are fragile, non‑portable, or destroy environment isolation. A native `uv` mechanism to handle system‑level GUI dependencies would greatly improve the user experience for the many developers and scientists who rely on interactive plotting on Linux.

Desired solutions could include:
- A way to automatically detect and expose system packages required for common GUI backends.
- A built‑in hook or plugin system (similar to `virtualenvwrapper`'s `postmkvirtualenv`) allowing users to run custom steps after venv creation.
- A command‑line flag to include specific system packages (more granular than `--system-site-packages`).
- Official documentation or a recipe that solves the “matplotlib + GTK/Qt on Linux” problem once and for all.

### Example

## Current behavior (broken)

$ pacman -Q python-gobject
python-gobject 3.56.2-1

$ uv venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
$ uv pip install matplotlib

$ python -c "import gi"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'gi'

$ python -c "import matplotlib; print(matplotlib.get_backend())"
agg

## Desired behavior

After a hypothetical `uv` command like `uv venv --with-system-gui` (or an equivalent hook), the same setup would work out of the box:

$ uv venv --with-system-gui   # or similar mechanism
$ source .venv/bin/activate
$ uv pip install matplotlib

$ python -c "import gi; print('gi loaded successfully')"
gi loaded successfully

$ python -c "import matplotlib; print(matplotlib.get_backend())"
GTK3Agg   # or any interactive backend

This would allow interactive matplotlib plots to appear immediately, without additional manual steps.

### Summary

I am building a Python GUI app through GitHub Actions for 3 platforms: Linux x86, MaxOS Arm and Windows x86. For that I use the managed runners ubuntu-latest, macos-latest and windows-latest. Specifically on Windows, I need to use an older version of the PyQt5 dependency, otherwise it won't build, so I described that on my [pyproject.toml](https://github.com/lima-emanuel/appstpa/blob/main/pyproject.toml):

```
    "pyqt5-qt5==5.15.2 ; sys_platform == 'win32' and platform_machine == 'AMD64'",
    "pyqt5==5.15.9 ; sys_platform == 'win32' and platform_machine == 'AMD64'",
    "pyqt5-sip==12.11.1 ; sys_platform == 'win32' and platform_machine == 'AMD64'",
    "pyqt5-qt5==5.15.18 ; sys_platform != 'win32'",
    "pyqt5==5.15.11 ; sys_platform != 'win32'",
    "pyqt5-sip==12.18.0 ; sys_platform != 'win32'",
```

I have also put the following on my `pyproject.toml`:

```
[tool.uv]
required-environments = [
    "sys_platform == 'win32' and platform_machine == 'AMD64'",
]
```

But, on the Windows build, `uv` ignores that and tries to build the app with `pyqt5-qt5==5.15.18`, which [fails](https://github.com/lima-emanuel/appstpa/actions/runs/25466900331/job/74722367904#step:5:31). On the other two platforms, it works. The error:

body_text:
**backstory**

I finally set a minimum release age (`exclude-newer`) in my global uv config (bc of the recent worm https://socket.dev/blog/tanstack-npm-packages-compromised-mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attack)

I excluded some personal packages from this cooldown, bc I do need the latest versions of those.

but now I discovered my user-configured exclusions were leaking into the `uv.lock`s of the projects I was working on: https://x.com/dasfacc/status/2055037715687645696

I work on the Pydantic AI repo, and this got me thinking that we should have a static check that prevents contributors from accidentally leaking _their_ exclusions into our `uv.lock`, and more importantly, have CI flag exclusions: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/5446

**realization**

then I learned that project config takes precedence over user/system config, and package-specific cooldown overrides can weaken a user’s global cooldown policy, which made me think we should have tools to prevent that kind of behavior, given our new security climate.

that’s why I’m opening this issue. I had codex provide examples and snippets so we can discuss possibilities, if you agree with the proposal.

thank you for your time and your work!

David

---

For example, a user might configure:

```toml
exclude-newer = "7 days"
```

But a project can add an override such as:

```toml
[tool.uv]
exclude-newer-package = { some-package = false }
```

or otherwise use a newer/more permissive cutoff for a package. That may be legitimate for private packages, security fixes, or operational exceptions, but it can also bypass the user's intended minimum release age policy.

It would be useful to have a user/system-level setting that controls what happens when project-level or lockfile-level cooldown settings weaken the user's configured policy.

### Example


```toml
# ~/.config/uv/uv.toml
exclude-newer = "7 days"

dependency-cooldown-override-policy = "deny" # allow | warn | deny

[[dependency-cooldown-override-allow]]
projects = ["~/work/pydantic-ai/**"]
repositories = ["https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai"]
packages = ["pydantic-harness"]
override-types = ["disable", "relax"]

[[dependency-cooldown-override-allow]]
projects = ["~/work/experiments/**"]
packages = [":all:"]
override-types = ["relax"]
```

The exact names are not important, but possible names include:

- `dependency-cooldown-override-policy`
- `exclude-newer-override-policy`
- `release-age-override-policy`
- `warn-on-exclude-newer-override`

The important behavior is:

- `allow`: current behavior
- `warn`: continue, but warn when a project weakens the user/system cooldown policy
- `deny`: fail unless the override matches an allow rule

An override would be considered weakening if it allows versions that the user/system cooldown would otherwise exclude, for example:

- disabling the cooldown for a package with `exclude-newer-package = { name = false }`
- using a shorter relative cooldown for a package
- using a newer absolute cutoff for a package
- possibly applying a more permissive per-index cooldown, if relevant

Allow rules probably need to match both where the override is coming from and what package it applies to. A project-only allowlist is too broad: I may trust a specific repository to override cooldowns for `pydantic-harness`, but not to bypass the policy for arbitrary packages.

The `repositories` field would be optional convenience. A path matcher is probably the clearest local security boundary, while repository matching could use normalized VCS remote URLs to allow any worktree of a trusted repository.

The exact schema is illustrative. If this followed existing uv conventions, `packages` might use package names plus an all-packages sentinel like `:all:` rather than shell-style `*`.

NOTE: I found the workaround for this issue with a claude.ai session and I have generated parts of this issue's text with claude.

---

## Summary

`uv lock` resolved `greenlet 3.5.1` at a moment when only one of its ten wheels had reached PyPI (the macOS freethreaded build). The remaining wheels -- linux x86_64, musllinux, win_amd64, win_arm64, etc. -- landed within five minutes. The lock file is frozen on that partial snapshot.

`uv sync` on a Linux CPython 3.15 host then fails with:

```
hint: You're using CPython 3.15 (`cp315`), but `greenlet` (v3.5.1) only has
wheels with the following Python ABI tag: `cp315t`
```

even though `cp315-cp315-manylinux_2_24_x86_64.manylinux_2_28_x86_64` wheel has been released in the meantime.

## Reproduction

1. Trigger `uv lock` (fresh checkout, `uv sync`, `uv add foo`) while an upstream dependency's release is mid-upload -- only some platform wheels published, others still being pushed by per-platform CI runners.
2. `uv` locks the wheels currently visible on PyPI's JSON index.
3. The remaining wheels land within seconds/minutes.
4. The lock file contains a single-platform wheel pin for a multi-platform package.
5. `uv sync` on any excluded platform fails with the ABI-tag hint above.

### Concrete data — `greenlet 3.5.1`

PyPI upload times (via `curl https://pypi.org/pypi/greenlet/json | jq`):

| Upload time (UTC)   | Filename                                                             |
|:--------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 2026-05-20 13:10:19 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-macosx_11_0_universal2.whl`             |
| 2026-05-20 13:12:07 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315-macosx_11_0_universal2.whl`              |
| 2026-05-20 13:13:15 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315-win_amd64.whl`                           |
| 2026-05-20 13:13:37 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-win_arm64.whl`                          |
| 2026-05-20 13:13:59 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-win_amd64.whl`                          |
| 2026-05-20 13:14:32 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315-manylinux_2_24_x86_64.…2_28_x86_64.whl`  |
| 2026-05-20 13:14:35 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-manylinux_2_24_x86_64.…2_28_x86_64.whl` |
| 2026-05-20 13:14:42 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315-musllinux_1_2_x86_64.whl`                |
| 2026-05-20 13:14:43 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-musllinux_1_2_x86_64.whl`               |
| 2026-05-20 13:15:37 | `greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315-win_arm64.whl`                           |

`uv lock` ran between 13:10 and 13:12 and captured only the first wheel.

### Resulting lock entry

```toml
[[package]]
name = "greenlet"
version = "3.5.1"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
wheels = [
    { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/.../greenlet-3.5.1-cp315-cp315t-macosx_11_0_universal2.whl", ... },
]
```

One wheel. macOS-only. Freethreaded-only.

## Actual behaviour

`uv lock` silently produces a lock file that works on exactly one platform/ABI combination. The failure surfaces later, on a different machine, as a confusing ABI-tag error during `uv sync`.

## Expected behaviour

`uv lock` warns when a freshly-resolved version's wheel set is much smaller than the previous release's wheel set for the same package — e.g. `greenlet 3.5.0` ships ~60 wheels, `3.5.1` ships 1. That delta is a near-certain signal of an in-progress upload, detectable from the index alone without any user configuration, and the warning can recommend `--upgrade-package <name>` after the release settles.

`uv` should also maybe recommend defining an expected environment and error if no such wheel is found during a lock / upgrade.

## My Current Workaround

Quickfix:

```sh
uv lock --upgrade-package greenlet
```

Yet may happen again in future upgrades / locks.

I furthermore realized I could declare the platforms the project must support, so `uv lock` refuses to produce a lock missing a compatible wheel for any declared environment:

```toml
[tool.uv]
required-environments = [
  "sys_platform == 'linux' and platform_machine == 'x86_64'",
]
```

This may be something that `uv` should require / recommend to the user to define for their project to guarantee that it only upgrades to proper channels.

## Affected package:

- `greenlet 3.5.1`, pulled in transitively via `playwright 1.60.0`

## Related issue

- [#14885  `uv` attempts to install the newer version if one has been released while `uv` is running](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/14885)

### Platform

 Linux x86_64 (WSL2 Debian Trixie)

### Version

uv 0.11.15 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

### Python version

Python 3.15.0b1

---

## Summary

`uv lock` resolved `greenlet 3.5.1` at a moment when only one of its ten wheels had reached PyPI (the macOS freethreaded build). The remaining wheels -- linux x86_64, musllinux, win_amd64, win_arm64, etc. -- landed within five minutes. The lock file is frozen on that partial snapshot.

`uv sync` on a Linux CPython 3.15 host then fails with:

```
hint: You're using CPython 3.15 (`cp315`), but `greenlet` (v3.5.1) only has

even though `cp315-cp315-manylinux_2_24_x86_64.manylinux_2_28_x86_64` wheel has been released in the meantime.

## Reproduction

1. Trigger `uv lock` (fresh checkout, `uv sync`, `uv add foo`) while an upstream dependency's release is mid-upload -- only some platform wheels published, others still being pushed by per-platform CI runners.
2. `uv` locks the wheels currently visible on PyPI's JSON index.
3. The remaining wheels land within seconds/minutes.
4. The lock file contains a single-platform wheel pin for a multi-platform package.
5. `uv sync` on any excluded platform fails with the ABI-tag hint above.

```toml

name = "greenlet"
version = "3.5.1"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }

```

One wheel. macOS-only. Freethreaded-only.

## Actual behaviour

`uv lock` silently produces a lock file that works on exactly one platform/ABI combination. The failure surfaces later, on a different machine, as a confusing ABI-tag error during `uv sync`.

## Expected behaviour

`uv lock` warns when a freshly-resolved version's wheel set is much smaller than the previous release's wheel set for the same package — e.g. `greenlet 3.5.0` ships ~60 wheels, `3.5.1` ships 1. That delta is a near-certain signal of an in-progress upload, detectable from the index alone without any user configuration, and the warning can recommend `--upgrade-package <name>` after the release settles.

`uv` should also maybe recommend defining an expected environment and error if no such wheel is found during a lock / upgrade.

```toml
[tool.uv]
required-environments = [
  "sys_platform == 'linux' and platform_machine == 'x86_64'",
]
```

This may be something that `uv` should require / recommend to the user to define for their project to guarantee that it only upgrades to proper channels.

### Summary

Initially I install a package with `uv pip install pkg<2`. When there is another invocation `uv pip install tool>2`, uv silently reinstalls this version, even if it conflicts with the previous requirement.

This also shows up in real-world usage: in [Zephyr](https://zephyrproject.org) projects, the install flow does `uv pip install $(west packages pip)`, and a second `uv pip install <more-packages>` run later against the same venv can silently change package versions pinned by the first invocation — because `uv pip install` only treats the currently-installed version as a soft preference for the *current* resolve, with no memory of what was explicitly required in a previous call. This isn't caught at install time; it only surfaces later, at runtime, when the mismatched version breaks something, by which point it's hard to trace back to which install call caused it.

Expected behavior: a later `uv pip install` invocation whose requirement directly contradicts an earlier invocation's requirement should fail fast with a resolution conflict, the same way it would if both specifiers had been passed to a single `uv pip install` call — not silently succeed and leave the environment in a state that contradicts an earlier, still-relevant requirement.

uv's current default behavior (treating the installed version as a soft preference, not a hard constraint) shouldn't change, since plenty of workflows rely on being able to freely change versions across separate install calls. This is why an opt-in flag — analogous to `git commit --amend` — could make sense: `--amend` could consider previous invocations' explicit requirements as constraints, while plain `uv pip install` keeps behaving exactly as it does today. Alternative naming could be `--safe`

### Example

```
uv pip install "tool>=1.0,<2"   # resolves to e.g. tool==1.8.0
uv pip install "tool<=1.7"       # correctly downgrades to tool==1.7 (matches this call's own spec)
uv pip install "tool>=2"         # silently installs tool==2.5 — no error, even though this
                                  # directly contradicts the very first invocation's <2 constraint
uv pip install --amend "tool<2"         # fails, as this directly contradicts the >=2 constraint
```

Real Life example:

```
user@machine:~/work/Temp/uv-example$ uv pip install west==1.5.0
Resolved 9 packages in 549ms
Installed 9 packages in 19ms
 + colorama==0.4.6
 + docopt==0.6.2
 + packaging==26.3
 + pykwalify==1.8.0
 + python-dateutil==2.9.0.post0
 + pyyaml==6.0.3
 + ruamel-yaml==0.19.1
 + six==1.17.0
 + west==1.5.0

user@machine:~/work/Temp/uv-example$ uv pip install pyyaml==3.10
Resolved 1 package in 1.19s
      Built pyyaml==3.10
Prepared 1 package in 137ms
Uninstalled 1 package in 0.62ms
Installed 1 package in 0.69ms
 - pyyaml==6.0.3
 + pyyaml==3.10
```

As a result `west` will fail during runtime, as it calls functions from incompatible version `pyyaml 3.10`.

I'd love to have a flag like `--amend` or `--safe` so I can be sure that the installation does not break anything as all previous constrains are still considered.

body_text:
### Summary

In my experience, I've typically needed to include license information for each component in an SBOM. This functionality currently does not exist in `uv export --format cyclonedx-1.5`. It appears that an optional license field already exists in the component struct used to generate the SBOM but it is always set to None.

I'm not too familiar with how the export receives package information but my quick skim didn't show any easily accessible means of obtaining the license from a given Package. The only struct I could find that contains such information is `Metadata23` and it wasn't clear to me how that could be made available to the export.

I'm also not sure how easy it is to acquire this information without having the package downloaded. Pypi exposes this through their API but I don't know if that sort of API is available through any index or just pypi. And direct url dependencies wouldn't provide such an API either, potentially forcing a wheel download just to obtain the necessary metadata. Still, that seems preferable to having to fully sync the project as would be required by a tool like cyclonedx-bom.

body_text:
### The value of integrating

`crates/uv-performance-memory-allocator` says its own purpose plainly: pull in mimalloc on Windows and tikv-jemallocator on most other platforms. So uv already treats the allocator as a performance decision worth a dedicated crate, and already carries two C allocators to make it — each needing a C toolchain on the platforms it covers.

rusty_alloc is not a different design being offered as an alternative: it is the mimalloc v2.4.5 algorithm rebuilt in safe Rust, implementing about 150 of mimalloc's roughly 157 `mi_*` entry points, with the C original kept in-tree purely as a differential oracle. So on the Windows arm this is the same algorithm, and it would let one entry replace both arms rather than adding a third.

That matters for what uv does. Resolution builds and discards a large graph of candidate versions, and installation unpacks and writes thousands of small files, with `rayon = "1.10.0"` spreading both across a pool — so allocations are routinely freed on a worker that did not make them. On exactly that path the rusty_alloc README measures **0.83x mimalloc's instructions** (`xthread` — every free performed by a non-owning thread). It has 9,261 downloads on crates.io and no build script.

Not asking you to change the default — this would sit behind an off-by-default feature in that same crate.

### How to integrate

```toml
[features]
rusty-alloc = ["dep:rusty_alloc-api"]   # opt in; the mimalloc/jemalloc arms stay as they are

[dependencies]
rusty_alloc-api = { version = "2.1", optional = true }
```

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "rusty-alloc")]
#[global_allocator]
static GLOBAL: rusty_alloc_api::RustyAlloc = rusty_alloc_api::RustyAlloc;
```

Nothing else changes: same resolver, same lockfile, same CLI. Because it is pure Rust it needs no per-platform toolchain, so one arm could eventually cover Windows, macOS and Linux alike — which is the part worth measuring even if the ratios come out level.

### Remade With Rust & MATA

We are rebuilding the C libraries Rust projects still depend on, in safe Rust — allocators, codecs, compression, parsers, identity and storage — so a build can drop its C pieces without losing performance. The org is at https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust. If this is not for you, please close the issue.

rusty-alloc = ["dep:rusty_alloc-api"]   # opt in; the mimalloc/jemalloc arms stay as they are

[dependencies]
rusty_alloc-api = { version = "2.1", optional = true }
```

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "rusty-alloc")]
#[global_allocator]
static GLOBAL: rusty_alloc_api::RustyAlloc = rusty_alloc_api::RustyAlloc;
```

Nothing else changes: same resolver, same lockfile, same CLI. Because it is pure Rust it needs no per-platform toolchain, so one arm could eventually cover Windows, macOS and Linux alike — which is the part worth measuring even if the ratios come out level.

### Remade With Rust & MATA

We are rebuilding the C libraries Rust projects still depend on, in safe Rust — allocators, codecs, compression, parsers, identity and storage — so a build can drop its C pieces without losing performance. The org is at https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust. If this is not for you, please close the issue.

Using a symlink cache is the only way to prevent wastage of disk space for a machine with multiple projects.

Different projects may have different dependencies and when some are upgraded, the previous version is left behind unused in the cache. This is wasteful for disk space.

The current operations allowed for cache handling are mostly related to full-blown purge which would require a re-download of previously downloaded packages. These network transfers are wasteful.

It would be useful to have specific commands that allow the following:
- they list what packages+versions are in the cache
- allow purging individual package+version combinations
- less importantly: a way to exhamine how much disk space is being used by every cached package+version combination

thank you and keep up with the great work.

### Summary

#### Summary
Provide a straightforward way to modify (add, remove, or update) additional dependencies (`--with`) associated with an already installed tool without requiring users to manually reconstruct the original installation command.

---

#### Problem Statement
Currently, `uv tool install <package> --with <dep>` allows users to inject extra dependencies at install time, and `uv tool list --show-with` allows inspecting them. 

However, once a tool is installed, there is no direct, low-friction path to alter its set of extra dependencies. The current workaround requires reinstalling the main tool while manually reproducing all original options alongside the revised `--with` arguments. Even with `uv tool list --show-xxx`, reconstructing the exact original installation invocation is manual and error-prone.

---

#### Use Case: Plugin Management
A widespread pattern in the Python ecosystem involves CLI applications that rely on modular, third-party plugin packages (for example, `ocrmypdf`, `pytest`, or `flake8`). 

In these ecosystems:
1. **Plugins must reside in the same environment** as the primary executable to be discovered at runtime.
2. **Plugins are installed incrementally:** Users frequently discover, install, update, or remove plugins long after the core tool was first installed.
3. **Plugins vary in source:** They may come from PyPI, VCS repositories, or local `.whl` files.

Because plugins are developed independently, users need an easy way to treat an installed `uv tool` environment as a target for adding or removing auxiliary packages over time.

---

#### Additional Context
* **Real-world example:** `ocrmypdf` heavily relies on separate plugin packages installed into the same environment.
* Supporting post-install dependency management will make `uv tool` a much more versatile replacement for isolated CLI tools with rich plugin ecosystems.

### Example

#### Proposed Solutions / UX Suggestions

Introduce explicit management commands targeting an installed tool's environment:

```bash
# Add or update one or more dependencies/plugins to an existing tool environment
uv tool alter <tool> --add-with <package>
# or possibly, to update only if already existing,
uv tool alter <tool> --update-with <package>

# Remove a dependency/plugin from an existing tool environment
uv tool alter <tool> --remove-with <package>
```

### Summary

When `XDG_DATA_HOME` is set, `install.sh` derives its install directory as the literal string `$XDG_DATA_HOME/../bin` and never resolves it. Because two later checks compare that string against a resolved path, they result in:

1. Spurious `WARN: The following commands are shadowed by other commands in your PATH: uv uvx` on every install, when nothing is shadowed.
2. The `PATH`-modification step concludes the install dir isn't on `PATH` when it is, and appends source lines to six shell config files that didn't need them.

The second one is self-reinforcing: the line it adds prepends the unnormalized path to `PATH`, which guarantees the warning fires on every subsequent run, including runs with an explicit `UV_INSTALL_DIR`.

## Environment

- `uv 0.12.17 (635500036 2026-09-18 aarch64-apple-darwin)`
- macOS 27.0 (build 26A428, Darwin 27.0.0, arm64)
- `XDG_DATA_HOME=$HOME/.local/share`
- `$HOME/.local/bin` already on `PATH`, added by my own shell config
- `zsh`, with `ZDOTDIR=$HOME/.config/zsh`
- No other uv on the system (no Homebrew formula, no cargo install, one binary total)

## Reproduction

```zsh
$ export XDG_DATA_HOME="$HOME/.local/share"
$ export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
$ curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

downloading uv 0.12.17 aarch64-apple-darwin
installing to /Users/me/.local/share/../bin
  uv
  uvx
everything's installed!
WARN: The following commands are shadowed by other commands in your PATH: uv uvx
```

`which -a uv` returns exactly one path. Nothing is shadowed.

The install also appended `. "$HOME/.local/share/../bin/env"` to `~/.profile`, `~/.bashrc`, `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.zshrc/`. `~/.zshenv`, and created `~/.config/fish/conf.d/uv.env.fish` and `~/.config/fish/`  on a machine with no fish installed.

I would have expected no warning, and no shell config modified, since there was no `uv` binary installed on the device and `$HOME/.local/bin` is already on `PATH`.

## Cause

`install.sh:1298` sets the install dir without resolving the path:

```shell
_install_dir="$XDG_DATA_HOME/../bin"
```

`check_for_shadowed_bins (install.sh:1434)` then compares a resolved path against that raw string.

```shell
_shadow="$(command -v "$_bin_name")"        # /Users/me/.local/bin/uv
if [ -n "$_shadow" ] && [ "$_shadow" != "$_install_dir/$_bin_name" ]; then
    # /Users/me/.local/share/../bin/uv  →  never equal
```

The same string is used for the already-on-`PATH` check at `install.sh:1401`.

```shell
case :$PATH: in *:$_install_dir:*) NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 ;;
```

`PATH` contains `/Users/me/.local/bin`, not `/Users/me/.local/share/../bin`, so this never matches and `shotgun_install_dir_to_path` (`install.sh:1409`) runs against `.profile` `.bashrc` `.bash_profile` `.bash_login`

Reinstalling with `UV_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin"`, even after rm -rfing the binaries still warns, because the rc line added by the first run is now prepending `$HOME/.local/share/../bin` to PATH in every shell. `command -v uv` resolves through the unnormalized entry and the comparison fails again. The only fix is manually removing the line the installer added, which is non-trivial to track down.

## Suggested fix

Normalize once, at the point the default is chosen with something like

```shell
_install_dir="$(cd "$XDG_DATA_HOME/.." 2>/dev/null && pwd)/bin"
```

This would make the shadowing check and the $PATH$ check agree, and the `NO_MODIFY_PATH=1` branch at line 1401 then correctly suppresses all six rc edits on systems where the directory is already on `PATH`.

### Separately, and lower priority

creating `~/.config/fish/` on a machine with no fish binary seems worth gating on `command -v fish`, and writing to `.bashrc`, `.bash_profile`, and `.bash_login` unconditionally is more invasive in my opinion than the situation calls for. I'd personally rather be told which line to add than have it added for me. That said, the path resolution bug is the actionable part here, and fixing it means the rc files mostly stop being touched at all.

### Platform

macOS 27.0 (build 26A428, Darwin 27.0.0, arm64)

### Version

uv 0.12.17 (635500036 2026-09-18 aarch64-apple-darwin)

### Python version

Python 3.14.7

{"repository": "astral-sh/uv", "task_candidate_id": 2085, "repository_id": 39, "issue_number": 21837, "github_issue_id": 5511820847, "html_url": "https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/21837", "created_at": "2026-09-19T16:38:09+00:00", "author_association": null, "title": "`install.sh` unresolved `$XDG_DATA_HOME/../bin` causes false "shadowed by other commands" warning and unnecessary rc-file edits", "body_text": "### Summary

When `XDG_DATA_HOME` is set, `install.sh` derives its install directory as the literal string `$XDG_DATA_HOME/../bin` and never resolves it. Because two later checks compare that string against a resolved path, they result in:

1. Spurious `WARN: The following commands are shadowed by other commands in your PATH: uv uvx` on every install, when nothing is shadowed.
2. The `PATH`-modification step concludes the install dir isn't on `PATH` when it is, and appends source lines to six shell config files that didn't need them.

The second one is self-reinforcing: the line it adds prepends the unnormalized path to `PATH`, which guarantees the warning fires on every subsequent run, including runs with an explicit `UV_INSTALL_DIR`.

## Environment

- `uv 0.12.17 (635500036 2026-09-18 aarch64-apple-darwin)`
- macOS 27.0 (build 26A428, Darwin 27.0.0, arm64)
- `XDG_DATA_HOME=$HOME/.local/share`
- `$HOME/.local/bin` already on `PATH`, added by my own shell config
- `zsh`, with `ZDOTDIR=$HOME/.config/zsh`
- No other uv on the system (no Homebrew formula, no cargo install, one binary total)

## Reproduction

```zsh
$ export XDG_DATA_HOME="$HOME/.local/share"
$ export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
$ curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

downloading uv 0.12.17 aarch64-apple-darwin
installing to /Users/me/.local/share/../bin
  uv
  uvx
everything's installed!
WARN: The following commands are shadowed by other commands in your PATH: uv uvx
```

`which -a uv` returns exactly one path. Nothing is shadowed.

The install also appended `. "$HOME/.local/share/../bin/env"` to `~/.profile`, `~/.bashrc`, `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.zshrc/`. `~/.zshenv`, and created `~/.config/fish/conf.d/uv.env.fish` and `~/.config/fish/`  on a machine with no fish installed.

I would have expected no warning, and no shell config modified, since there was no `uv` binary installed on the device and `$HOME/.local/bin` is already on `PATH`.

## Cause

`install.sh:1298` sets the install dir without resolving the path:

```shell
_install_dir="$XDG_DATA_HOME/../bin"
```

`check_for_shadowed_bins (install.sh:1434)` then compares a resolved path against that raw string.

```shell
_shadow="$(command -v "$_bin_name")"        # /Users/me/.local/bin/uv
if [ -n "$_shadow" ] && [ "$_shadow" != "$_install_dir/$_bin_name" ]; then
    # /Users/me/.local/share/../bin/uv  →  never equal
```

The same string is used for the already-on-`PATH` check at `install.sh:1401`.

```shell
case :$PATH: in *:$_install_dir:*) NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 ;;
```

`PATH` contains `/Users/me/.local/bin`, not `/Users/me/.local/share/../bin`, so this never matches and `shotgun_install_dir_to_path` (`install.sh:1409`) runs against `.profile` `.bashrc` `.bash_profile` `.bash_login`

Reinstalling with `UV_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin"`, even after rm -rfing the binaries still warns, because the rc line added by the first run is now prepending `$HOME/.local/share/../bin` to PATH in every shell. `command -v uv` resolves through the unnormalized entry and the comparison fails again. The only fix is manually removing the line the installer added, which is non-trivial to track down.

## Suggested fix

Normalize once, at the point the default is chosen with something like

```shell
_install_dir="$(cd "$XDG_DATA_HOME/.." 2>/dev/null && pwd)/bin"
```

This would make the shadowing check and the $PATH$ check agree, and the `NO_MODIFY_PATH=1` branch at line 1401 then correctly suppresses all six rc edits on systems where the directory is already on `PATH`.

### Separately, and lower priority

creating `~/.config/fish/` on a machine with no fish binary seems worth gating on `command -v fish`, and writing to `.bashrc`, `.bash_profile`, and `.bash_login` unconditionally is more invasive in my opinion than the situation calls for. I'd personally rather be told which line to add than have it added for me. That said, the path resolution bug is the actionable part here, and fixing it means the rc files mostly stop being touched at all.

### Platform

macOS 27.0 (build 26A428, Darwin 27.0.0, arm64)

uv 0.12.17 (635500036 2026-09-18 aarch64-apple-darwin)

```shell

uv workspace add
uv workspace remove

uv workspace lock
uv workspace run
uv workspace tree

On a Linux HPC environment, importing torch failed with
`ImportError: libnccl.so.2: cannot open shared object file`.
`nvidia_nccl_cu13-2.30.7.dist-info` existed and its `RECORD` listed
`nvidia/nccl/lib/libnccl.so.2` at 252,204,648 bytes, but the entire
`nvidia/nccl/` directory was absent. Repeating `uv sync --frozen` did not
restore it or report the missing library.

`uv sync --frozen --reinstall-package nvidia-nccl-cu13` restored the library
at the recorded size. Our setup script now checks `import torch` before
marking the environment verified, and the package cache has been moved
away from the quota-limited home filesystem.

The home filesystem was full around the incident. That is a suspected
trigger, not an established cause: we did not preserve the original
installation output, exact uv/Python versions, or a reproducer of the file
loss. We cannot establish whether installation, a corrupt cache, or a later
operation removed the files. The observed behavior is that a subsequent
sync accepted the incomplete environment. Is there a supported way to
detect missing installed files without forcing a reinstall?

Related reports checked before drafting:

- https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/16468 describes missing package files
  after remove/add on macOS, but also a missing RECORD; our RECORD existed.
- https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/19683 was closed after a clean cache
  resolved missing files. We have not established whether that cause applies.

### Summary

Windows 10 1903+ and Windows 11 ship with the “app execution alias” mechanism. App Installer (DesktopAppInstaller) registers:

%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps\python.exe

%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps\python3.exe

uv python install <version> --default adds the path to the user PATH, but that has lower priority than the invalid python alias above.

Can --default instead add its path to the system PATH?

body_text:
### Summary

For filesystems with inode quotas, it would be helpful to know how many inodes the uv cache is using, e.g.

```console
$ uv cache size --inodes
12345
```

This is particularly relevant to HPC clusters, which often have strict inode limits.

To implement this, I'm guessing the place to start would be an upstream PR into diskus to expose inode counts. I'd be happy to work on this, but first I wanted to see if uv would be interested in this functionality.

If the idea is acceptable, there are lots of little UI decisions to be made, for example:
- Should the default (human readable) display use a suffix like 12.3K to match the byte counts?
- Should the parameter be named `--inodes` or `--count` or ...?
- Should the default display show size \*and\* count?

### Summary

Installing a differently named package for the same module (e.g. `xgboost-cpu` installed over `xgboost`) seems unrelated in the conflict resolution. 

Doing a manual remove of the old package, deletes a bunch of files in the site-package module as well.

### Expected behaviour:
- recognize different packages for same module -> having both `xgboost` requirement should have been a conflict in the first place, I believe
- do not remove module files that belong to another installation -> can only be recovered with a `--reinstall[-package]`

### Steps to reproduce:

### Summary

When using `uv sync --frozen`, I want to be able to override the location from which packages are installed (defined  in URLs in my frozen uv.lock file) using the `UV_INDEX` environment variable or the `--index` command line argument. This is particularly useful in air-gapped networks or on networks where pypi.org/pythonhosted.org are unreachable. I think this behavior should also apply to `uv run --frozen <cmd>` when the auto-syncing of packages occurs. In my case, not being able to override the indexes is forcing me to manually manage my venv in my air-gapped network, which half defeats the purpose of using uv. 

I have a repository that is mirrored to an air-gapped network. My uv.lock file is built and committed to my project repo on an internet facing machine before being mirrored. The python dependencies for building/running the project are mirrored to a GitLab python registry that in no way matches the paths within my lock file (pypi.org/pythonhosted.org). Rebuilding my lock file on the air-gapped network is not feasible because not all dependencies for all groups and all python versions are mirrored on the air-gapped network, just the versions for the version of python I'm using.

Design details:
- In order for packages from overridden indexes to be synced, they need to match the name, version and hash from the uv.lock file
- Index overrides take precedence over the URL listed in the lock file. If they don't exist, fall back to the URL in the lock file
- The lock file will not be modified because the `--frozen` flag is in use in these cases


### Example

When a user is using a frozen uv.lock file in an air-gapped network or on a corporate network using a proxy PyPi registry, currently they must manually manage their virtual environment because `uv sync --frozen` will refuse to accept index overrides. With the requested changes, a user could set up some environment variables (UV_INDEX and optionally UV_INDEX_MYINDEX_USERNAME and UV_INDEX_MYINDEX_PASSWORD) and then `uv sync --frozen` and `uv run --frozen <cmd>` would behave and sync dependencies as if the user were on the internet. The user would no longer have to manually manage the virtual environment.

```
export UV_INDEX=myindex=https://mygitlab.org/api/v4/projects/4/packages/pypi
export UV_INDEX_MYINDEX_USERNAME=<gitlab-username>
export UV_INDEX_MYINDEX_PASSWORD=<gitlab-personal-access-token>

uv sync --frozen
```
In this example, uv would try to sync dependencies listed in the uv.lock file from `https://mygitlab.org/api/v4/projects/4/packages/pypi` first and then fall back to the URL listed in the uv.lock file.


### Example Code Changes
Here are some example code changes: https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/compare/main...rxanp:uv:rxanp/allow-index-override-on-sync

### Summary

When running [uv-installer.ps1](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/releases/download/0.12.23/uv-installer.ps1) in Windows with `HTTPS_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` environment variables used:

- HTTPS_PROXY value is used.
- NO_PROXY value is discarded.

This is an issue for my organisation, as internal assets cannot be accessed through the proxy, and we use an internal mirror for `UV_INSTALLER_GITHUB_BASE_URL`.

The part that fails is:
`function WebProxyFromEnvironment {
    $httpsProxy = [System.Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("HTTPS_PROXY")
    $allProxy = [System.Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("ALL_PROXY")
    $proxyUrl = if (-not [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($httpsProxy)) { $httpsProxy } else { $allProxy }
    $webProxy = WebProxyFromUrl -ProxyUrl $proxyUrl
    return $webProxy
}`

One correction could be (maybe with added null check):
`function WebProxyFromEnvironment {
    $httpsProxy = [System.Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("HTTPS_PROXY")
    $allProxy = [System.Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("ALL_PROXY")
    $noProxy = [System.Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("NO_PROXY")
    $proxyUrl = if (-not [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($httpsProxy)) { $httpsProxy } else { $allProxy }
    $webProxy = WebProxyFromUrl -ProxyUrl $proxyUrl -BypassList $noProxy
    return $webProxy
}`

My team would be happy to contribute with your approval: however, i cannot find the source code for the standalone installer. 

### Platform

Windows 11 x64

### Version

0.12.23

### Summary

### **Problem Statement / Background**

Currently, PEP 735 dependency groups allow including other groups using `{ include-group = "group-name" }`. However, unlike standard dependency specifications (e.g., `package; python_version <= '3.13'`), there is no way to attach **environment markers** (such as `python_version` or `platform_system`) to an `include-group` entry.

This creates a limitation when composing larger optional dependency groups (like `all` or `dev`) that include platform-specific or Python-version-restricted optional dependencies.

---

### **Use Case**

Consider a project configured as follows:

```toml
[dependency-groups]
libtorrent = [
    "libtorrent~=2.1",
]

all = [
    { include-group = "libtorrent" },
    # other optional groups...
]

```

* `libtorrent` does not support **Python 3.14+**.
* If a user explicitly requests to install the `libtorrent` group (`uv sync --only-group libtorrent`) on Python 3.14, it **should fail** as expected.
* However, if a user requests to install the `all` group (`uv sync --group all`) on Python 3.14, we want `uv` to **silently skip** the `libtorrent` group instead of failing resolution due to the incompatible Python version restriction.

Without marker support on `include-group`, it is impossible to conditionally inherit dependency groups based on Python versions or operating systems.

---

### **Proposed Solution / Feature Request**

Allow environment markers to be specified on `{ include-group = ... }` declarations (or support inline marker syntax), similar to how markers work for standard package dependencies.

**Proposed Syntax Options:**

1. **Inline string marker syntax:**
```toml
[dependency-groups]
all = [
    { include-group = "libtorrent; python_version <= '3.13'" },
]

```


2. **Or structured table fields (if preferred for TOML consistency):**
```toml
[dependency-groups]
all = [
    { include-group = "libtorrent", marker = "python_version <= '3.13'" },
]

```

body_text:
## Summary

Currently `uv auth` supports only static credentials. Modern infrastructure frequently supports authentication routines to be handled using the short-living tokens. This also is specifically useful if later the `Bearer` auth scheme will be implemented. Dynamic credentials can be injected with `keyring`, but this hardly can be called reliable.

This feature request proposes an approach to introduce the support for external token vending app different from `keyring`. The motivation, analysis and example of the implementation spec are provided below.

If the approach is supported I will be glad to attempt contributing this.

## Detailed Proposal

The pluggable credential providers is not new and there are similar issues and requests already touching the scope. See e.g. (#19025, #7660), but this requests attempts to address some concerns on security side mentioned in the discussions. There are also existing workarounds that allow to enable this "sideways".

The further proposal text is structured as follows: I start with the use cases, then proposal and finally with the alternatives review. But there's no design decision yet that either promise the implementation or block it.

### Use cases

In enterprise environments and specifically with cloud services the access might be managed with a short-lived tokens. Users usually posess the tool/script/routine that obtains or refreshes required tokens. In majority of cases tokens are passed in `Bearer` scheme by adding it to HTTP headers. But if the identity provider is in place it's usually not difficult to tweak the ingress to validate the tokens in the HTTP basic schema.

### Proposal Specification

Add the following functionality with no strong opinion on exact naming of the flags/options

- `uv auth login --token-provider "{command}" {service}` allows to store the `{command}` decomposed into the call + arguments array.
- During the authentication loop `uv` performs a call for the provided command and streams the output as HTTP basic with `__token__` username by default.
- **Optional implementation details**. 
    - `--username` is still allowed and overrides `__token__`.
    - Feature flag to turn on/off the functionality (if needed, alike `native-auth`)
- **Caching**. AFAIK current `uv` authentication workflow doesn't support probes for staleness, so if the token is cached and expired - auth will fail. The exact approach to caching might be a design discussion, baseline - no caching or few seconds caching, or more advanced with configurable lifetime. I have no strong preference, but believe it's not a blocker.
- **Security**. The vending call is done with user impersonation and execute arbitrary code without sandbox. So few points:
    - **Prohibited as part of code**. No way to specify the `token-provider` as part of any configuration provided with code. The approach does not support anything but explicit local setup using `uv auth login` call. Handling such settings as part of `pyproject.toml/uv.toml` should be prohibited by design decision.
    - **Truncate output**. Output of the vending command is truncated by some (maybe configurable) max length.
    - **Prevent leaks to logs**. Vending call response is not logged.
    - **Protect config store**. If the vending call is stored as plain text in the credentials store - there's a risk that a third-party code will mutate the settings after `uv auth` calls. So storing in native store might be a better option, but require JSON support.
    - **No dynamic context**. Vending command is bound to service URL suffix, but user is responsible to path fixed service context as part of vending call definition if needed.
    - **Not a string**. Stored as command + arg list.

 ### Existing alternatives

1. **Wrappers/shims**. In this approach the actual `uv` command call is wrapped by adding a manual `UV_INDEX_{NAME}_PASSWORD` setup. E.g.

    ```sh
    UV_INDEX_EXAMPLE_PASSWORD=$(token-provider-cli -t service_name ...) path/to/uv
    ```    

    To wrap users either use `alias` approach or create a shell script that calls `uv`. This approach suffers from few problems regarding scaling:

    - Using identically named script like `uv` that calls `uv` is not considered a good practice. It requires `PATH` modification and also binds the exact path to `uv` (to avoid cycles).
    - Using differently named scripts breaks agentic coding experience as they are well trained to use `uv`.
    - Using aliases doesn't work in non-interactive sessions.
    - Suffers in enterprises as exact approach is OS-dependent.

2.  **Keyring**. There's a path to actually quickly generate a trivial `keyring` backend that will do the wrapping of the call to a token vendor. This is a closest alternative. But let's look at configuration efforts. E.g. assume the user is fine with having `keyring` as a global `uv tool`.

    ```sh
    # install keyring with custom backend
    uv tool install keyring --with {my_backend_path}

    # further configuration of keyring might be needed (priority of backends)
    ```

    This is what outlines the experience with this approach:
    - `keyring` is famous to have unstable behavior in Linux. Since keyring initializes all backends on every call - it may fail on system keyring backend even if it's not used.
    - `{my_backend_path}` will either have to be a GIT direct link or a PyPI.org package. The reason is that we are avoiding the chicken-egg problem, we cannot install packages from private indexes yet. Publishing to PyPI.org is not always preferrable, having GIT link technically works, but requires the user to set up authentication for non-public GIT index.
    - Mess with priorities. Some users might use `keyring` somewhere else, so changing priorities globally is unwanted as they might want to have priority of system keyring higher. That will ensure that we lose time on the call to system keyring, and in case of stale old credentials stored in the system keyring chaining to our custom backend won't happen.

    With all the difficulties, this is still a closest option to enable scalable configuration for enterprises.

## Final notes

The design spec is a **proposal**, not requirement. The proposal is based on the assumed architectural design decision that we aim to simplify and unify auth management on `uv` side, without necessity to use third-party packages. **Clarification of the direction is really appreciated**.

The proposal duplicates (correlates) with (#19025, #7660), but slightly differently defines the mechanism. Also no decision is taken in the mentioned items.

The implementation likely should wait for the #18907 to complete, as it might rely on the features that are already seen in Draft.

I'm eager to attempt contributing this if the proposal is supported.

## Example

Example is OS specific, I use MacOS. The `get_token_cli` is a custom application assumed to be available in the user machine. This is also an ideal one that assumes no feature flags required.

```sh
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# bearer (if ever) or basic with `__token__` username.
uv auth login --token-provider "get_token_cli -t pypi.company.com ..." pypi.company.com
```

For the cases the HTTP authentication requires non `__token__` username
```sh
# basic with custom_username
uv auth login \
  --token-provider "get_token_cli -t pypi.company.com ..." \
  --username custom_username \
  pypi.company.com
```

Now taken that configuration for the private index is provided in `uv.toml` or `pyproject.toml` (context dependent) user is ready to authenticate against a private index with a dynamic token.

### Summary

Suppose someone adds an entry to `constraint-dependencies` due to some bug in an indirect dependency. Then, they upgrade to a new version of the direct dependency which removes that indirect dependency, or remove the direct dependency entirely. Doing so won't remove the `constraint-dependencies` entry. If nobody notices it, it is possible this `constraint-dependencies` entry may linger long after it has ceased to serve any purpose.

What if there was a setting like `require-use-dependencies = true`, which would trigger an error if an individual constraint in `constraint-dependencies` (or `build-constraint-dependencies` or `override-dependencies`) wasn't actually used? That would mean, when you removed the indirect dependency, `uv lock` would fail?

Or maybe this is more like a lint rule for `uv check` (if that did more than just run `ty`)? Or for `ruff check` (if you were to add uv-specific lint rules)?

body_text:
## Summary

The same flag, `--from`, produces two different caching behaviors depending only on the source type it points to, with nothing in the command or its output distinguishing them. A local path (`--from <path>`) is cached forever with no mtime/content check (reported and closed as working-as-intended in #16196). A git source (`--from git+<url>`) is never cached in that sense at all - unpinned, pinned to a branch, or pinned to a tag, it re-resolves and rebuilds on every invocation, picking up changes even when a branch or tag is moved after the fact. Same interface, same intent ("use this source"), one source type gets rechecked every time and the other never does. That's a behavioral inconsistency, and it's what actually caused the #16196 report: the user had no way to know their source type was the one that doesn't get rechecked.

## The premise is misleading

uv's own README describes `uvx` as:

> Run a tool in an ephemeral environment using `uvx`

"Ephemeral" reads as "nothing persists between runs." For a local-path `--from`, the build is cached indefinitely, with no mtime or content check, and every subsequent invocation of the same command silently reuses that cached build even after the source has changed. That's a direct contradiction of the word used to describe it, not an approximation of it.

The response to #16196 was "please consult the uv documentation - these statements don't reflect what is actually implemented." That's fair for the bug report's suggested fixes, but it cuts both ways: the README's "ephemeral" framing *also* doesn't reflect what's implemented, for the exact same reason.

## Git sources are not cached at all; only local paths are

Confirmed by testing directly (not assumed), using a throwaway local git repo as a stand-in for a remote. Every git ref form re-resolves and rebuilds on every single invocation, with no flags needed:

- **Unpinned** (`--from git+file://$PWD`, floats to HEAD): new commit on the default branch -> next run picks it up.
- **Pinned to a branch name** (`--from git+file://$PWD@mybranch`): new commit pushed to that branch -> next run picks it up.
- **Pinned to a tag** (`--from git+file://$PWD@v1.0`), even force-moved to a different commit: next run picks up the new commit the tag now points to.
- Pinned to a literal commit SHA is the one case with nothing to re-resolve, since a SHA can't change by definition.

Minimal repro for the unpinned case (the branch/tag cases follow the same shape - pin with `@name`, move the ref, rerun):

```bash
git init pkg && cd pkg
echo 'def main(): print("VERSION-1")' > probe.py
# ...minimal pyproject.toml with a `probe` entry point...
git commit -am v1

uvx --from "git+file://$PWD" probe   # -> VERSION-1

echo 'def main(): print("VERSION-2")' > probe.py
git commit -am v2

uvx --from "git+file://$PWD" probe   # -> VERSION-2, same command, no flags
```

Every git ref type gets rechecked on every invocation; a local path never does, regardless of ref type. uv already does the correct thing - recheck the source before reusing a build - for every form a git source can take, and specifically carves out local paths from that same check. That reads like local paths were simply never wired into the recheck path that every git ref already goes through, not like a deliberate design decision that local paths should be cacheable.

## How we independently ran into this

We hit the identical failure mode ourselves while building a small local package (a few hundred lines) that itself depends on a separate project via `git+https://...`. The git dependency was never a problem, for the reasons above; the local package was.

It took exactly two restarts to notice, and the first wasn't conclusive on its own. After editing the source and restarting the long-running daemon with `uvx --from . <cmd>`, its output still showed pre-edit text - confusing, but explainable away (an old instance still running in the background, something not saved, etc.). Restarting it a second time produced the exact same stale output again, and that's what made it clear something was being cached where no caching was expected.

## Ask

Primarily: treat the inconsistency itself as the bug. Either local-path sources should get the same re-resolve-on-invocation behavior git sources already get (so `--from` means the same thing regardless of source type), or, if that's intentionally not going to change, `uvx` should say so at the point of use - e.g. a one-time notice the first time it caches a local-path build, not silence.

Secondarily, and regardless of which fix is taken: the README's description of `uvx` as running a tool "in an ephemeral environment" is true for git/PyPI sources and false for local-path sources as currently implemented, so it shouldn't be stated as a blanket claim about the tool.

Related: #16196

That's fair for the bug report's suggested fixes, but it cuts both ways: the README's "ephemeral" framing *also* doesn't reflect what's implemented, for the exact same reason.

## Git sources are not cached at all; only local paths are

Confirmed by testing directly (not assumed), using a throwaway local git repo as a stand-in for a remote. Every git ref form re-resolves and rebuilds on every single invocation, with no flags needed:

- **Unpinned** (`--from git+file://$PWD`, floats to HEAD): new commit on the default branch -> next run picks it up.
- **Pinned to a branch name** (`--from git+file://$PWD@mybranch`): new commit pushed to that branch -> next run picks it up.
- **Pinned to a tag** (`--from git+file://$PWD@v1.0`), even force-moved to a different commit: next run picks up the new commit the tag now points to.
- Pinned to a literal commit SHA is the one case with nothing to re-resolve, since a SHA can't change by definition.

Minimal repro for the unpinned case (the branch/tag cases follow the same shape - pin with `@name`, move the ref, rerun):

```bash
git init pkg && cd pkg
echo 'def main(): print("VERSION-1")' > probe.py
# ...minimal pyproject.toml with a `probe` entry point...
git commit -am v1

uvx --from "git+file://$PWD" probe   # -> VERSION-1

echo 'def main(): print("VERSION-2")' > probe.py
git commit -am v2

uvx --from "git+file://$PWD" probe   # -> VERSION-2, same command, no flags
```

Every git ref type gets rechecked on every invocation; a local path never does, regardless of ref type. uv already does the correct thing - recheck the source before reusing a build - for every form a git source can take, and specifically carves out local paths from that same check. That reads like local paths were simply never wired into the recheck path that every git ref already goes through, not like a deliberate design decision that local paths should be cacheable.

## How we independently ran into this

We hit the identical failure mode ourselves while building a small local package (a few hundred lines) that itself depends on a separate project via `git+https://...`. The git dependency was never a problem, for the reasons above; the local package was.

It took exactly two restarts to notice, and the first wasn't conclusive on its own. After editing the source and restarting the long-running daemon with `uvx --from . <cmd>`, its output still showed pre-edit text - confusing, but explainable away (an old instance still running in the background, something not saved, etc.). Restarting it a second time produced the exact same stale output again, and that's what made it clear something was being cached where no caching was expected.

## Ask

Primarily: treat the inconsistency itself as the bug. Either local-path sources should get the same re-resolve-on-invocation behavior git sources already get (so `--from` means the same thing regardless of source type), or, if that's intentionally not going to change, `uvx` should say so at the point of use - e.g. a one-time notice the first time it caches a local-path build, not silence.

Secondarily, and regardless of which fix is taken: the README's description of `uvx` as running a tool "in an ephemeral environment" is true for git/PyPI sources and false for local-path sources as currently implemented, so it shouldn't be stated as a blanket claim about the tool.

## Summary

`uv run --no-project` ignores the current project but still uses the local `.python-version` file at the **root of the current workspace**, overriding the global Python version configured by `uv python pin --global`.

Please make `--no-project` ignore the workspace-root `.python-version` and use the global pin from `~/.config/uv/.python-version` instead.

Normal `uv run` commands should continue respecting the workspace-root `.python-version`, while an explicit `--python` argument should always take precedence.

## Description

On Windows, `uv self update` fails when `ALL_PROXY` is configured with a SOCKS5 proxy. The updater fails to download the new version because the download mechanism used by the Windows installer does not support the `socks5://` proxy scheme.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install a version of `uv` older than the latest available release (e.g. `0.13.3` when testing against `0.13.4`).
2. Configure `ALL_PROXY` to use a SOCKS5 proxy.
3. Run `uv self update` in PowerShell.

```powershell
$env:ALL_PROXY = "socks5://127.0.0.1:9050"
uv self update
```

The update must have a newer version available; otherwise, `uv self update` will report that it is already up to date without attempting the download.

## Actual behavior

The update fails while downloading the new version:

```text
info: Checking for updates...
error: The installation failed. Output from the installer: downloading uv 0.13.4 (x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
failed to download from https://releases.astral.sh/github/uv/releases/download/0.13.4
  failed to download https://releases.astral.sh/github/uv/releases/download/0.13.4/uv-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip to
       ...\uv.zip: The ServicePointManager does not support proxies with the socks5 scheme.
trying alternative download URL
failed to download from https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/releases/download/0.13.4
  failed to download https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/releases/download/0.13.4/uv-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip to
       ...\uv.zip: The ServicePointManager does not support proxies with the socks5 scheme.
failed to download binaries
```

The command exits with code `2`. Both the primary download URL and the GitHub fallback fail with the same error.

## Expected behavior

`uv self update` should be able to download and install updates when `ALL_PROXY` points to a SOCKS5 proxy, consistently with SOCKS5 support in `uv`'s own HTTP client.

## Additional verification

I reproduced the failure with two installed versions:

| Installed version | Update target | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `0.11.8` | `0.13.4` | Fails |
| `0.13.3` | `0.13.4` | Fails |

In the same environment, I was able to download and run `uv 0.13.4` through `uvx`:

```powershell
uvx uv --version
# uv 0.13.4 (7456b60bc 2026-10-20 x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
```

This suggests that the failure is specific to the standalone self-update download path, rather than a general inability to download or execute `uv` through the configured proxy.

## Possible cause

The Windows PowerShell installer appears to use .NET's `System.Net.WebClient` and `System.Net.WebProxy` for downloading the release archive. This mechanism rejects the `socks5://` proxy scheme with the reported `ServicePointManager` error.

A SOCKS5-compatible download mechanism, or reuse of `uv`'s own HTTP client for the download, may resolve the issue.


### Platform

Windows 11 x86_64

### Version

uv 0.13.3 (502f93ca6 2026-10-19 x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)

### Python version

### Summary

I am trying to have a more generic environment + script management than `hatch`, `nox`,` tox`, etc. PEP723 scripts come close to this, but they don't have clear support for project extras or dependency groups.

The project extras can potentially be solved with using the `project[extra]` syntax and/or the path navigation. The issue would be, how to convey that this dependency should be installed as editable?

Dependency groups are more unclear since there is no format for defining these as dependencies.

There is the [`tool.uv.tasks`](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/5903) proposal, but this just shifts the definition from `hatch` to `uv` and still end up locked to an environment. My preference here is to use the standards defined for it PEP723 being the case here, and somehow extend the definition or settings to tell the runner `uv`/`hatch` etc. how to prepare an environment and reuse the definitions given in `pyproject.toml`. For example

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# [tool.environment]
# name = "docs"
# root = ".."
# dependency-groups = ["docs"]
# ///
```

### Workaround

### Summary

When uv fetches a Git dependency into its cache database, `git fetch` can start Git's automatic maintenance in the background (`git maintenance run --auto --detach`). Since Git 2.54 the default maintenance strategy is geometric repacking, which writes a multi-pack-index and deletes the packs it replaced. uv then immediately runs `git clone --local` (or `--no-hardlinks` after a failed `--local` attempt) from that same database into a checkout. The clone and the detached maintenance can overlap, and the clone can fail with `No such file or directory` for a pack or for `multi-pack-index.lock`.

We hit this twice in CI (GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners, uv 0.13.4 via `astral-sh/setup-uv`, Git 2.55.0) while installing a project twice in one job from a local `git+file://` URL, so the second install fetched into the existing cache database:

```text
error: Git operation failed
  cause: process didn't exit successfully: `/usr/bin/git clone --no-hardlinks /home/runner/work/_temp/setup-uv-cache/git-v1/db/18a968a57034ee11 /home/runner/work/_temp/setup-uv-cache/git-v1/checkouts/18a968a57034ee11/edec79c` (exit status: 128)
         fatal: failed to copy file to '/home/runner/work/_temp/setup-uv-cache/git-v1/checkouts/18a968a57034ee11/edec79c/.git/objects/pack/pack-e8ff1962efa64c3d6618ca63f5bed9a75de43537.pack': No such file or directory
```

```text
error: Git operation failed
  cause: process didn't exit successfully: `/usr/bin/git clone --no-hardlinks /home/runner/work/_temp/setup-uv-cache/git-v1/db/18a968a57034ee11 /home/runner/work/_temp/setup-uv-cache/git-v1/checkouts/18a968a57034ee11/96152b7` (exit status: 128)
         fatal: failed to copy file to '/home/runner/work/_temp/setup-uv-cache/git-v1/checkouts/18a968a57034ee11/96152b7/.git/objects/pack/multi-pack-index.lock': No such file or directory
```

### What we traced

We could not reproduce the failure itself locally (81 traced and untraced installs all succeeded), so the link between these two CI failures and maintenance is inferred from the mechanism below rather than observed in a failing run.

With uv 0.13.4 and Git 2.55.0 (built from the official source), a second install from the same URL produced this Trace2 sequence (paths shortened):

```text
git fetch --force --update-head-ok file:///<source> +<sha>:refs/commit/<sha>
git maintenance run --auto --no-quiet --detach
git repack -d -l --cruft --cruft-expiration=2.weeks.ago --write-midx
git clone --local <uv-cache>/git-v1/db/<id> <uv-cache>/git-v1/checkouts/<id>/<rev>
git multi-pack-index write --no-progress --preferred-pack=pack-<hash>.pack ... --stdin-packs
```

A syscall trace of one install (with maintenance forced to run) shows the overlap directly: the clone linked a pack from the database, then about 37 ms later the detached repack unlinked that same pack, with `multi-pack-index.lock` created and renamed in between. In that sample the clone had already copied the file, so it succeeded; a slightly different interleaving gives the errors above.

Relevant upstream facts:

- Git 2.54 release notes: "git maintenance" starts using the "geometric" strategy by default.
- `maintenance.autoDetach` falls back to `gc.autoDetach` and defaults to true.
- The `git clone` documentation warns that a local clone "can race with concurrent modification to the source repository".
- In uv 0.13.4 and 0.13.5, `fetch_with_cli` in `crates/uv-git/src/git.rs` runs `git fetch --force --update-head-ok` without disabling automatic maintenance, and `clone_into` clones from the database right afterwards.

### Suggestion

Since uv owns the cache database and clones from it immediately, consider disabling automatic maintenance for uv's own fetches, for example `git fetch --no-auto-gc` (available since at least Git 2.23; a synonym of `--no-auto-maintenance` since Git 2.29), or `-c maintenance.auto=false -c gc.auto=0`. If periodic maintenance of the database is wanted, it could run explicitly while uv holds its cache lock.

Workaround we use in the meantime: run uv with `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`GIT_CONFIG_KEY_n`/`GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_n` entries setting `maintenance.auto=false` and `gc.auto=0`. With that, the same sequence shows the fetches with no maintenance child.

### Versions

- uv 0.13.4 (CI); the relevant code is unchanged in 0.13.5
- Git 2.55.0 (CI and local reproduction of the overlap); Git 2.53.0 did not run the geometric repack by default
- Linux x86_64
